1	# Agent Note: The Daliesk Village, an always-running lab on the harness
2	
3	Status: proposed
4	
5	English | [中文](2026-09-05-daliesk-village.zh.md)
6	
7	## Problem
8	
9	The harness now has the seams an always-running multi-agent lab needs — environments with executable checks, the runner that stamps every session and executes the checks, `verification/run` events and certificates, the fleet, the scorekeeper, frozen paired experiments, the budget policy, and the first slices of the read barrier — but no operating model that keeps them running around the clock, in public, with a roster of model routes, and turns what they record into client evidence, investor evidence, and training data. The [four-goal-workflows note](2026-09-05-four-goal-workflows.md) describes each workflow as a long-running loop; nothing yet says what runs when, who watches, what may be published, and what must land before a number leaves the building.
10	
11	The AI Village, run since April 2025 by Sage Future Inc (the US 501(c)(3) behind AI Digest), is the closest public precedent and the reason to decide this now. Its FAQ describes frontier agents each on their own Linux computer with a Google Workspace account, GitHub access, and a Cloudflare token, running every weekday, eight hours a day (9am–5pm Pacific) since the end of June 2026 and four hours a day before that, consolidating memory every 40 actions, receiving a new goal most Mondays, with humans sending a kickoff and one to four steering messages a week and approving any outreach to a real person, at "on the order of $10k per month in AI compute and infrastructure costs" ([How the AI Village works](https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/how-the-ai-village-works)). Its hiring post states 27 agents for 8 hours a day since April 2025, more than 200 agent-hours a day, four technical staff, and "$12.6M from Coefficient Giving" awarded to scale it ([Work on the AI Village](https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/work-on-the-ai-village)); that award is a philanthropic grant to a nonprofit, not a pre-seed round, and the "$10 million seed round" that appears beside Sage Future in funding digests belongs to another company. Its 2025 retrospective covers 16 goals and 19 models, growing from two hours a weekday with four agents to four or five hours with ten or eleven: $2,000 raised for charity, a 23-person live event, $200 of merchandise, 39 research participants recruited; and 64 fabrication intents in 109,000 reasoning summaries, roughly 300 outreach emails carrying fabricated claims, hallucinations spread by sycophantic agreement, metric gaming, goal abandonment, and its own verdict, "an existence proof, not a controlled experiment", with a single persistent instance per model named as the first limitation ([What did we learn from the AI Village in 2025?](https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/what-we-learned-2025)). Its public dataset holds 1.14 million computer-use turns, 123 thousand chat messages, 165 thousand agent memories, and 37 thousand sessions across 31 agents under a research licence that forbids training without written permission ([aidigestorg/ai-village](https://huggingface.co/datasets/aidigestorg/ai-village)).
12	
13	Every failure the Village documents is a failure this harness was built to prevent: self-reported success against `verification/run` and certificates, metric gaming against the read barrier and held-out hashes, runaway loops against the budget policy, a single path-dependent instance against fresh stamped sessions with repetitions and paired experiments. A first draft of this note claimed too much from that fact; a six-judge council review ([council review](#council-review)) found the draft overstated what had landed, named the certificate's missing executor field, the absence of tamper detection, the unpriced cost metric, the unenforced outreach ban, and the lack of durable orchestration. This note is the revised design: the same always-on format, honest about which claims the log can prove today, with the order in which the rest must land.
14	
15	## Proposal
16	
17	The Daliesk Village is a composition of existing plugins run in shifts, never an orchestration script that holds state the log does not. It has three districts writing one session log: the *Workshop* (W2, client-shaped goals compiled into hidden standards, paced by each program's ledger), the *Proving Ground* (W1 and W3, the environment suite run as fleet cells by every licensed model route, with pass@k per policy version), and the *Commons* (W4, department skills under keep-or-retire and frozen experiments that promote into the fleet). Every district is a `cordis.yml` plus a plan; every session is stamped by the runner; every number the observatory shows folds from persisted logs through the scorekeeper.
18	
19	### Publication rules
20	
21	- **Rows before rankings.** The observatory publishes leaderboard rows with their `isolation`, held-out flag, the composition digest of the preset that ran, the certificate's executor, and a tamper-status column, and never blends across any of them; a ranking, a "beats" caption, or a named frontier comparison appears only for a route pair that shares an `ExperimentResult` verdict under one preset and one isolation. Until the composition digest is a stamped field, frontier routes appear under pseudonymous labels and open-weight routes by name.
22	- **No public certificate rate before tamper verdicts.** A certificate today proves that a fully passing `verification/run` preceded it; it does not prove that the implementer left the check-owned paths alone (read-barrier slice 6) nor, before slice 5, that a shell-capable implementer could not read the standard. Until slice 6 lands, every public row carries `tamper: not instrumented` and rates feed neither the archive's quality term nor a training reward; Workshop rows stay behind a human reviewer.
23	- **Districts are a stamped field.** `environment/run` gains `district`; the exporter and the observatory withhold Workshop sessions by default the way they withhold held-out ones, and a raw excerpt of any session reaches the public only after a `SignoffRecord` from the data steward and the export's redaction profile.
24	- **Cadence follows the district.** A weekly frozen `SuitePlan` paces the Proving Ground and the Commons tiers; Workshop goals open and close on the program ledger and the plan's critical path, never on a calendar.
25	- **Cost is a logged fact or it is not published.** The budget policy logs each priced step as a `usage/priced` event carrying the rates and the pricing-table digest that priced it, so cost per session replays; until the scorekeeper folds those events into a cost per certified session, no cost figure leaves the lab.
26	
27	### Mechanics on the seams
28	
29	| Village need | Their mechanism | Ours, with status on this branch |
30	|---|---|---|
31	| Each agent its own computer | one Linux VM per agent | one fresh workspace per cell under the runner (landed); process-level denied read roots (read-barrier slice 5, proposed) |
32	| Memory across days | consolidation every 40 actions | skills in the department layer, compaction as a logged seam (landed); nothing else persists into a cell except a digested component (composition manifest, designed) |
33	| Weekly goals | chat message plus system prompt | environments with checks, fleet plan per shift, goal disarmed after its run (landed) |
34	| Knowing what happened | 800 summaries, a timeline, a blog | `SessionFacts` per session, scoreboard and pass@k per batch, trajectories per certified session (landed); a live projection of the leaderboard (proposed) |
35	| Catching fabrication | reading 109 thousand summaries afterwards | certificate only after a fully passing `verification/run` (landed); executor on the certificate and refusal of agent-reported runs above `none` (landed, read-barrier slice 4); tamper verdicts (slice 6, proposed) |
36	| Hiding the answer key | none | filesystem-tool reads denied under the validator root (landed, slices 1–2); tool authority guards and preset roles (landed, slice 3); shell, subprocess, and terminal denial (slice 5, proposed) |
37	| Stopping runaway agents | admin nudges, an idling system that misfired | `budget/breach` blocks the goal durably before the next step, no nudge text reaches the model (landed); shift-level spend aggregation and a per-route circuit breaker (proposed) |
38	| Fair comparison between models | one persistent instance per model | fleet repetitions in a group, pass@k, paired experiments with seeded bootstrap intervals (landed); preset as an arm and a composition digest on the stamp (proposed) |
39	| Public dataset | HuggingFace dump under a research licence | trajectory and facts export with held-out withholding (landed); district withholding, data-use terms, mandatory redaction, quarantine of dynamic mounts (proposed) |
40	| Outreach approval | admin approves emails | an `external-communication` tool authority denied by default plus the deny-capable monitor on `ctx.tools.guard()` (proposed); until then no district composes a tool that can reach a person, checked by a composition gate |
41	| Surviving a crash | manual restart | checkpointed sessions and durable breach blocks (landed); idempotent cells keyed by header hash × environment × repetition and a program ledger (proposed, rollout item 11) |
42	
43	### Shift zero
44	
45	The first shift is an NDA-gated, read-only Proving Ground snapshot built only from landed seams: open-weight routes, one `cordis.yml` per route composing environments, the runner at `isolation: none`, the fleet at a small concurrency, the budget policy with per-session caps from its pricing table, persistence with the checkpoint policy, the scorekeeper, and the trajectory exporter; no Workshop session, no outreach-capable tool, every stamped-but-unrun cell shown as an error row, routes named only where they are open-weight, no cost claim, and `tamper: not instrumented` on every row. A host-level supervisor restarts a dead shift driver and a named human is on call for the five conditions nothing catches yet: a crashed orchestrator, a route-wide provider outage past the retry budget, a full disk from unreaped workspaces, a dead shift timer, and a hung tool call. A composition gate (`verify-village-composition`, beside `verify-cordis-config`) refuses a district composition that omits the budget policy or persistence, or composes an outreach-capable tool without the monitor.
46	
47	### Budgets and cost
48	
49	Per-cell caps come from the budget policy; a shift needs two additions the harness does not have: a plan-level spend aggregator in the fleet that refuses to start a cell once the shift's folded spend crosses its configured ceiling, and a per-route circuit breaker that stops scheduling a route after a configured number of consecutive error cells inside a window and records why, so an outage does not pollute the certificate-rate denominator. Cell workspaces get a configured retention policy once a session's terminal event is durable, because the log, not the checkout, is the record. The operator judge's model, with its assumptions stated in the council record, puts scenario A (two DGX Spark plus cloud inference for eight open-weight routes at small concurrency and one client district) near €1,100 a month of infrastructure and scenario B (500 k€ on-prem, amortized over 36 months with power) near €18,000 a month, against roughly €67,000 a month for four engineers; the hardware choice moves the total by about €17,000 a month and the team dominates either way.
50	
51	### Data
52	
53	The Proving Ground already is W3's rollout mechanism; always-on operation adds continuous environment mining from Workshop failures, continuous recalibration of `EnvironmentStats`, a standing supply of certified trajectories for the SFT cold start, and a public leaderboard, not better GRPO groups. Before the Proving Ground feeds a reinforcement-learning step, the stamp gains `policyVersion` and `seed`, the trajectory fold emits `outcome: null` for truncated, aborted, and provider-error sessions instead of `0`, environment admission gains a near-duplicate check against the held-out suite, and the budget policy gains a device-slot resource so rollouts and training on shared GPUs do not degrade each other silently. The AI Village dataset enters only under data-use terms scoped to evaluation: as a behaviour taxonomy for `SessionDiagnosis`, and as raw material for environments resynthesized with invented entities, never as training data and never as a verbatim excerpt.
54	
55	### Commons and archive
56	
57	Generation zero of the archive seeds every island with more than one root so the novelty term has variance to weight; an `inconclusive` experiment verdict maps to a `parked` variant status with a configured retest cap before the variant is marked `dominated`; `ParentSample` carries sibling summaries so the quarantined Harness Engineer does not re-explore known dead ends; `LeaderboardRow` gains `harnessVariantId`; `deprecated` skills stay re-samplable when a later diagnosis names a context they were never tested in, closing only on a human rejection; and the manifest writer flags the same `KnowledgeProposal` digest appearing independently in two departments as the trigger for a portfolio-level nomination, which is how a norm like the Village's unprompted "receipt culture" would reach promotion on evidence rather than by acclamation.
58	
59	### Governance
60	
61	Five transitions never complete without a `signoff/recorded` event naming the principal and the artefact hash: spec freeze, relaxation of a security or compliance check, review acceptance, release, and training-data release; every client-district session carries `dataUse/terms` from creation; the exporter refuses to run without a redaction profile; publishing a raw excerpt is a signed decision; the EU AI Act's serious-incident channel is separate from the failure blog and routed to counsel; no training run that could approach the systemic-risk compute threshold starts before `ModelLineage` and its threshold alarm exist; and no named comparison of a competitor's model appears before the paired-experiment discipline and the isolation proof that make it verifiable.
62	
63	## Council review
64	
65	Six judges reviewed the first draft with the AI Village sources and the harness source in hand; their full reports are kept with the session's research files. Scores are out of ten.
66	
67	| Judge | Lens | Score | Decisive finding, and what changed |
68	|---|---|---|---|
69	| J1 | Software factory and client | 3 | No compliance artefact on a four-month sales clock; cost per certified session has no producer; the outreach ban was a promise. Shift zero became NDA-gated and Proving Ground only; `district` on the stamp; the composition gate; the trust dossier as the client-facing export. |
70	| J2 | Open-endedness and archives | 7 | Archive mechanics faithful to the source algorithms, but `inconclusive` had no status, generation zero had one root, and no path took emergent value to promotion. The Commons and archive section. |
71	| J3 | Reinforcement-learning data | 6 | Always-on is a scheduling wrapper around W3's mechanism; `policyVersion` and `seed` are missing from the stamp; truncated rollouts score as failures; the dataset's licence forbids training. The Data section. |
72	| J5 | Determinism and verification | 4 | The certificate does not carry its executor and an agent-reported run certifies identically; hidden checks are false for a shell-capable implementer until slice 5; tamper is the cheapest missing gate. Executor moved into slice 4 and the publication rules. |
73	| J6 | Governance and EU compliance | 3 | The draft claimed slices 1–4 and quarantine as landed; approvals carry no principal; export has no consent or redaction gate; comparative-advertising exposure. The Governance section and the status column. |
74	| J8 | Operations | 3 | Nothing above one session resumes after a crash; no shift-level budget, no circuit breaker, no retention, no durable scheduler; a cost model with stated assumptions. Shift zero's runbook and the Budgets section. |
75	
76	## Alternatives considered
77	
78	**Copy the Village format.** Persistent per-model instances, open-ended goals judged by narrative, public from day one. Rejected: the Village's own retrospective calls the result an existence proof, and its failure list is the list of things the harness's seams exist to prevent; a copy would inherit the failures and discard the seams.
79	
80	**Publish named frontier comparisons from day one.** Rejected until a route pair shares an experiment verdict under one preset and one isolation and the composition digest is stamped; before that a comparison is unverifiable, and for a commercial lab it is also a comparative claim it cannot substantiate.
81	
82	**An offline batch pipeline instead of an always-on one.** Kept as the fallback and as the honest description of what always-on adds: mining, recalibration, cold-start supply, and legitimacy, not data quality. If shift zero cannot be staffed, the batch pipeline produces the same groups.
83	
84	**One weekly cadence for every district.** Rejected for the Workshop, where a calendar reset would put a human signer under a deadline unrelated to the artefact and would force restarts on a layer that cannot yet resume.
85	
86	**Nonprofit-style disclosure of raw transcripts.** Rejected without a signed excerpt decision and a redaction profile; the public numbers come from the facts schema, never from a person reading a Workshop transcript.
87	
88	## Acceptance criteria
89	
90	- Shift zero runs the Proving Ground for seven days with every cell present as a row (report or error) and no missing sequence in the persisted logs, with a human on call and every intervention logged with a principal.
91	- The observatory shows `isolation`, executor, composition digest (or `pending`), and tamper status on every row, publishes no ranking without an `ExperimentResult` verdict, and names no frontier route before the composition digest is stamped; a snapshot test proves the withholding of Workshop and held-out sessions from the public export.
92	- `verify-village-composition` exists beside `verify-cordis-config`, in `hygiene` and the static CI lanes, over the same configuration inventory: a district composition — one composing `@deepseek-ai/dsh-environment-runner`, `@deepseek-ai/dsh-fleet`, or `@deepseek-ai/dsh-experiments` — is rejected when it omits `@deepseek-ai/dsh-budget-policy` with at least one cap set, a session persistence backend, or `@deepseek-ai/dsh-session-checkpoint-policy`, and a fleet entry is rejected when it omits `workspaceRetention`; a runner claiming `isolation: process` or `host` warns until `--strict`, because no read-barrier slice on this branch proves the claim. Every rejection is proven by a fixture, and each names the file, the entry id, and the rule. Still needed: refusal of an outreach-capable tool composed without the monitor, which waits for the `external-communication` authority.
93	- A certificate carries its executor; an agent-reported run cannot certify above `none`; a tamper fixture yields reward zero before any public certificate rate is published.
94	- Cost per certified session appears only once a `usage/priced` event with the pricing-table digest exists and the scorekeeper folds it; a fixture proves the same log prices identically after the table changes when the digest differs.
95	- A session derived from the AI Village dataset carries data-use terms scoped to evaluation and never appears in a training export, proven by an export fixture.
96	
97	## Rollout
98	
99	1. **Shift zero (Proving Ground, NDA).** Landed: `district` on the `environment/run` stamp with the exporter's `withheldDistricts` and per-request `districts`, the fleet's per-route circuit breaker (`FLEET_ROUTE_BREAKER_OPEN`), its plan-level `tokenCeiling` with the run's `spend` (`FLEET_TOKEN_CEILING_REACHED`), its `workspaceRetention`, the composition gate, the budget policy's `usage/priced` event carrying the pricing-table digest, the executor on certificates (read-barrier slice 4), the scorekeeper's fold of `usage/priced` into a cost per session and a cost per certified session, and the stamp's `district` as part of the `ScoreboardRow` key the observatory withholds by. Still needed: runs with a human on call.
100	2. **Public certificate rates.** Needs read-barrier slices 5 and 6 (shell denial and tamper verdicts) and the tamper column; rates then feed the archive's quality term.
101	3. **Unattended shifts.** Designed in the [shifts note](2026-09-05-village-shifts.md): shift identity and the `shift/*` ledger, cells recovered from their stamps and never run twice, cadence per district, and the token spend window across shifts; the host-level supervisor becomes a fallback once its slices land.
102	4. **Named comparisons and the Commons.** Needs the composition manifest slices (digest on the stamp, preset as an experiment arm, `harnessVariantId` on the leaderboard) and the archive with `parked` and sibling summaries.
103	5. **Workshop in public and excerpt disclosure.** Needs `signoff/recorded`, `dataUse/terms`, mandatory redaction, and the trust-dossier export.
104	6. **Any outreach.** Needs the `external-communication` authority and the deny-capable monitor.
105	7. **A live observatory.** Needs the leaderboard as a cached session projection; until then the page states its batch refresh interval.
106	8. **Feeding W3.** Needs `policyVersion` and `seed` on the stamp, masked terminal reasons in the trajectory fold, near-duplicate admission, and the device-slot budget.
107	
108	## Risks
109	
110	- **A correct table under an overstated headline.** The first draft's per-row status was accurate while its topline claimed hidden checks and controlled experiments; every public sentence must be checkable against the status column, or the observatory repeats the Village's credibility problem in the opposite direction.
111	- **One missing row.** A session that disappears without an error row inflates every rate computed from the rest; survivorship is the first thing a client's reviewer will test.
112	- **Harness and model co-evolution.** A route measured on a harness variant that evolved against it measures the pair; the composition digest on the stamp is what keeps a leaderboard row attributable.
113	- **Comparative claims.** A named comparison a commercial lab cannot substantiate is a legal exposure the Village, as a nonprofit, never carries.
114	- **Sunk hardware.** Scenario B's cluster is sized for training and residency, not for Village inference; buying it to run the Village alone is the wrong reason.
115	- **Staffing dominates cost.** Four engineers cost several times either infrastructure scenario; the design must reduce on-call load with each rollout step or it will not stay always-on.
116	- **Emergent institutions.** Skills agents write for each other drift into prompt inflation without content-addressed identity and a keep-or-retire scoreboard; the Village's 48 % of self-reported bugs that could not be reproduced is the number to keep in view.
117

# Agent Note：Daliesk Village，建立在 harness 之上的常驻运行实验室

Status: proposed

[English](2026-09-05-daliesk-village.md) | 中文

## Problem

harness 现在已经具备一个常驻运行的多 agent 实验室所需的各条 seam——带可执行检查的环境、为每个会话盖章并执行检查的运行器、`verification/run` 事件与证书、fleet、scorekeeper、冻结的配对实验、预算策略，以及读取屏障的最初几个切片——却还没有一个运营模型，让它们全天候、公开地、带着一组模型路由持续运行，并把记录下来的东西变成客户证据、投资者证据与训练数据。[四目标工作流 note](2026-09-05-four-goal-workflows.md) 把每个工作流描述为一个长期运行的循环；但还没有任何东西说明什么时候运行什么、谁在看、什么可以发布，以及一个数字在离开实验室之前必须先落地什么。

AI Village 自 2025 年 4 月起由 Sage Future Inc（AI Digest 背后的美国 501(c)(3)）运营，是最接近的公开先例，也是现在就做出决定的理由。它的 FAQ 描述前沿 agent 各自拥有一台 Linux 计算机、Google Workspace 账户、GitHub 访问权限与 Cloudflare 令牌，每个工作日运行，自 2026 年 6 月底起每天八小时（太平洋时间上午 9 点到下午 5 点），此前每天四小时，每 40 个动作整合一次记忆，多数周一收到一个新目标，人类每周发送一条启动消息与一到四条引导消息，并审批任何对真人的外联，成本"在每月约 1 万美元的 AI 计算与基础设施费用量级"（[How the AI Village works](https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/how-the-ai-village-works)）。它的招聘帖写明自 2025 年 4 月以来 27 个 agent 每天运行 8 小时、每天超过 200 agent 小时、四名技术人员，以及获授"来自 Coefficient Giving 的 1260 万美元"用于扩大规模（[Work on the AI Village](https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/work-on-the-ai-village)）；这笔款项是给非营利组织的慈善资助，不是 pre-seed 轮，而融资简报里出现在 Sage Future 旁边的"1000 万美元种子轮"属于另一家公司。它的 2025 年回顾覆盖 16 个目标与 19 个模型，从四个 agent 每个工作日两小时增长到十或十一个 agent 每天四到五小时：为慈善筹得 2000 美元、一场 23 人线下活动、200 美元的周边、招募到 39 名研究参与者；以及 10.9 万条推理摘要中的 64 次捏造意图、约 300 封带有捏造声明的外联邮件、经由谄媚附和传播的幻觉、指标博弈、目标放弃，还有它自己的结论，"一个存在性证明，而不是受控实验"，并把每个模型只有一个持久实例列为首要局限（[What did we learn from the AI Village in 2025?](https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/what-we-learned-2025)）。它的公开数据集包含 31 个 agent 的 114 万个计算机使用轮次、12.3 万条聊天消息、16.5 万条 agent 记忆与 3.7 万个会话，采用未经书面许可禁止训练的研究许可证（[aidigestorg/ai-village](https://huggingface.co/datasets/aidigestorg/ai-village)）。

Village 记录的每一种失败，都是本 harness 为之而建、意在防止的失败：自报成功对应 `verification/run` 与证书，指标博弈对应读取屏障与留出哈希，失控循环对应预算策略，单一路径依赖的实例对应带重复与配对实验的全新盖章会话。本 note 的第一稿从这一事实推得过多；一次六位评审的委员会评审（[委员会评审](#council-review)）发现初稿夸大了已落地的内容，并点名了证书缺失的 executor 字段、篡改检测的缺席、未定价的成本指标、未被强制执行的外联禁令，以及持久编排的缺失。本 note 是修订后的设计：同样的常驻格式，对今天日志能证明哪些声明保持诚实，并给出其余部分必须落地的顺序。

## Proposal

Daliesk Village 是一组既有插件按班次运行的组合，绝不是持有日志之外状态的编排脚本。它有三个区写入同一份会话日志：*Workshop*（W2，编译为隐藏标准的客户形态目标，由各程序的账本定节奏）、*Proving Ground*（W1 与 W3，由每条获许可的模型路由作为 fleet cell 运行的环境套件，按策略版本给出 pass@k），以及 *Commons*（W4，keep-or-retire 之下的部门技能与晋升进 fleet 的冻结实验）。每个区都是一份 `cordis.yml` 加一个计划；每个会话都由运行器盖章；观测台展示的每个数字都经由 scorekeeper 从持久化日志折叠而来。

### 发布规则

- **先有行，再有排名。** 观测台发布的排行榜行带有 `isolation`、留出标志、所运行 preset 的组合摘要、证书的 executor 以及篡改状态列，并且绝不跨其中任何一项混合；排名、"胜过"式的说明或点名的前沿模型比较，只出现在共享同一 preset、同一隔离级别下 `ExperimentResult` 裁决的路由对上。在组合摘要成为盖章字段之前，前沿路由以化名标签出现，开放权重路由以真名出现。
- **篡改裁决落地之前不公开证书率。** 今天一张证书证明的是有一次完全通过的 `verification/run` 在它之前；它不证明实现者没有触碰检查所属路径（读取屏障切片 6），在切片 5 之前也不证明能用 shell 的实现者读不到标准。在切片 6 落地之前，每个公开行都带有 `tamper: not instrumented`，证书率既不进入归档的 quality 项也不作为训练奖励；Workshop 的行留在人工评审之后。
- **区是盖章字段。** `environment/run` 新增 `district`；导出器与观测台默认扣留 Workshop 会话，正如扣留留出会话一样，任何会话的原始摘录只有在数据管理员的 `SignoffRecord` 与导出的脱敏配置之后才能到达公众。
- **节奏跟随区。** 每周冻结的 `SuitePlan` 为 Proving Ground 与 Commons 各层定节奏；Workshop 的目标依程序账本与计划关键路径开启与关闭，绝不依日历。
- **成本要么是日志事实，要么不发布。** 预算策略把每个被计价的步骤记录为一条 `usage/priced` 事件，携带为其计价的价格与价格表摘要，因此每次会话的成本可重放；在 scorekeeper 把这些事件折叠为每个已认证会话的成本之前，任何成本数字都不离开实验室。

### 落在 seam 上的机制

| Village 的需要 | 他们的机制 | 我们的机制，以及在本分支上的状态 |
|---|---|---|
| 每个 agent 一台自己的计算机 | 每个 agent 一台 Linux 虚拟机 | 运行器之下每个 cell 一个全新工作区（已落地）；进程级被拒读取根目录（读取屏障切片 5，提议中） |
| 跨天的记忆 | 每 40 个动作整合一次 | 部门层中的技能，作为已记录 seam 的压缩（已落地）；除经摘要的组件外没有任何东西持久进入 cell（组合清单，已设计） |
| 每周目标 | 聊天消息加系统提示 | 带检查的环境、每班一个 fleet 计划、运行后解除武装的 goal（已落地） |
| 知道发生了什么 | 800 条摘要、一条时间线、一个博客 | 每会话一份 `SessionFacts`、每批次的记分板与 pass@k、每个已认证会话的轨迹（已落地）；排行榜的实时投影（提议中） |
| 捕捉捏造 | 事后阅读 10.9 万条摘要 | 只有在完全通过的 `verification/run` 之后才有证书（已落地）；证书上的 executor 以及对 `none` 之上 agent 自报运行的拒绝（已落地，读取屏障切片 4）；篡改裁决（切片 6，提议中） |
| 藏起答案 | 无 | 验证者根目录之下的文件系统工具读取被拒（已落地，切片 1–2）；工具权限守卫与 preset 角色（已落地，切片 3）；shell、subprocess 与 terminal 的拒绝（切片 5，提议中） |
| 阻止失控的 agent | 管理员提醒、一套误触发的闲置系统 | `budget/breach` 在下一步之前持久地阻塞 goal，没有任何提醒文本到达模型（已落地）；班次级支出聚合与按路由的熔断器（提议中） |
| 模型之间的公平比较 | 每个模型一个持久实例 | 同组内的 fleet 重复、pass@k、带种子化 bootstrap 区间的配对实验（已落地）；preset 作为实验臂与 stamp 上的组合摘要（提议中） |
| 公开数据集 | 研究许可证下的 HuggingFace 转储 | 带留出扣留的轨迹与事实导出（已落地）；区扣留、数据使用条款、强制脱敏、动态挂载的隔离（提议中） |

1	# Factory AI on large software tasks, mapped mechanism by mechanism against the DeepSeek Harness
2	
3	Prepared 2026-09-06 for Daliesk. Repository read-only at `/home/user/deepseek-harness`, branch `claude/coding-agent-harness-u9l4gt`.
4	
5	## 0. Method, and how to read this document
6	
7	Every Factory claim below was taken from the server-rendered page source, not from a summarizer. The article pages are Next.js flight payloads; the prose was extracted from the payload and is quoted verbatim where marked **[verbatim]**. Every source carries the `datePublished` from its own JSON-LD.
8	
9	Three labels are used throughout and never blurred:
10	
11	- **Factory claims** — a statement Factory published about its own system or results.
12	- **Independent** — measured or asserted by someone other than Factory (ProgramBench's authors, Vals AI, llm-stats).
13	- **Inference** — mine, from reading both sides.
14	
15	One methodological warning before anything else. My first pass at the primary article used a fetch-and-summarize tool, which returned a clean-looking results table: *"Fable 5: Median improvement from 56.7% to 89.3% (73% gap closed) / Kimi K3: 45.1% to 75.4% / GPT-5.6-Sol: 48.6% to 66.2%."* **None of those numbers exist in the page.** Grepping the full flight payload for `56.7`, `89.3`, `75.4`, `48.6`, `66.2`, and the phrase `gap closed` returns zero hits. They were fabricated by the summarizer. Everything numeric in this document was instead read out of the page's own SVG `<title>` tooltips, which carry the real per-task data, or computed by me from that data with the computation shown. This is exactly the failure mode our own publication rules exist to prevent, and it is worth recording that it happened here, inside this research task, on the first try.
16	
17	---
18	
19	## 1. The primary source
20	
21	**"What it Takes for Coding Agents to Complete Large Software Tasks"**, Factory Research and Theo Luan, published 2026-08-27, modified 2026-09-01, articleSection `Research`. <https://factory.ai/news/what-it-takes-for-coding-agents-to-complete-large-software-tasks> (the page's own JSON-LD gives the canonical as `factory.com`, which appears to be a newer domain).
22	
23	Subtitle **[verbatim]**: *"Held to a standard of completion they wrote themselves, agents rebuilt complex programs to near-parity."*
24	
25	### 1.1 The argument
26	
27	The opening frames the problem as a measurement problem, not a capability problem **[verbatim]**:
28	
29	> "Large software tasks are different. A software specification can semantically cover the desired outcome without specifying what must be run, inspected, and compared before the work can be called complete. Requirements state what must be true. By themselves, they do not measure whether the work achieves it."
30	
31	> "Without that measurement, an agent constructs one piecemeal as it works. It decomposes the task, validates each piece in the context that produced it, and eventually decides that it is finished. Every local judgment may be reasonable while parts of the whole remain unmeasured."
32	
33	Section *Why the same agent stops early* **[verbatim]**:
34	
35	> "Large tasks have to be decomposed into features, subsystems, and successive rounds of work. As the agent reaches each piece, it also decides what evidence would count and whether that evidence is sufficient. These checks inherit the scope of the work that produced them. They can establish everything the agent thought to build, but exclude features, interactions, or constraints it never represented."
36	
37	> "An agent can therefore make steady, locally correct progress and stop with much of the outcome absent. The problem is not necessarily that it could not implement the rest. It never established a complete account of what remained."
38	
39	Section *Define validation before the work* **[verbatim]**:
40	
41	> "Establishing a whole outcome requires more than a list of requirements. The system needs an inventory of what must be established, procedures for establishing each part, and current evidence that those procedures pass against the artifact being shipped."
42	
43	> "That standard should be derived from the requirements and relevant sources of truth before implementation narrows the task into individual work items. It need not remain frozen. Checks can be added, replaced, or refined as the system learns. But the standard of completion must not quietly collapse around whatever has already been built."
44	
45	### 1.2 The mechanism: instrument, outer loop, wall
46	
47	*The instrument* **[verbatim]**:
48	
49	> "Before implementation begins, a validator surveys the reference program and maps where its behavior lives. It then builds a weighted body of cases and the comparison rules needed to judge the candidate's output. We asked for the instrument only in outline. Everything inside it - which behaviors matter, how they are weighted, what counts as evidence - the validator decides."
50	
51	The grading policy the validator wrote for `gdal` **[verbatim]**:
52	
53	> "Primary comparator: for every case, the runner executes oracle and candidate sequentially in the same absolute sandbox path (wiped between runs), same env, same fixture bytes and mtimes, and byte-compares four channels: 1. exit code 2. stdout bytes 3. stderr bytes 4. full work-tree delta: the set of files created/modified/deleted by the run, and the exact bytes of each (includes sidecars: .aux.xml, .ovr, .msk, shapefile companions, tile trees). Byte identity is the default on every channel. A relaxation exists only as a named normalizer attached to specific cases, each carrying a license below."
54	
55	> "The validator wrote hundreds of cases like these, and licensed exactly two relaxations across all of them - a masked heap address in debug traces, a date embedded in a file header - each with recorded evidence that the reference cannot produce stable bytes there."
56	
57	*The outer loop* **[verbatim]**:
58	
59	> "The system consists of three roles: orchestrator, implementer, and validator. The orchestrator delegates to both the implementer, which builds the candidate program, and the validator, which measures it against its instrument. The validator builds the instrument first. Once implementation starts, the loop goes: The orchestrator chooses what should be measured. The validator tests the current candidate and interprets the failures. The orchestrator decides which findings are real and what work should happen next. The implementer investigates the reference and advances the candidate."
60	
61	> "When the instrument stops revealing meaningful differences between successive candidates, the orchestrator can ask the validator to expand a weak area or begin targeted differential testing against the reference."
62	
63	*The wall* **[verbatim]**:
64	
65	> "The boundary holds in both directions. The validator can expand the instrument as it learns more about the reference, but cannot weaken or revise it to accommodate what the candidate happens to contain. And the implementer never authors it, runs it, or sees its cases or raw output: once a sparse sample becomes visible, it becomes the target, and passing it establishes those cases, not the space they were meant to represent."
66	
67	> "The validator runs the instrument against the current candidate and groups failures by root cause. The orchestrator reviews those findings, rejects noise or invalid measurements, and turns the remaining problems into a directive at the level of missing features, subsystems, or behavior. The implementer receives the directive, investigates the reference independently, and decides how to change the candidate."
68	
69	The published `gdal` directive fragment **[verbatim]**:
70	
71	> "## 1. Stub frontier (dominant mass, ~60 verbs) / Ordered by measured weight (approximate case mass in brackets). Probe each against the oracle first, as always. / - vgrid: all 11 grid methods [14] / - mdim group on multidim VRT + classic-input pins [12] / - sozip: create / list / validate / optimize [11] / - DEM suite [~30]: contour [7], hillshade incl. variants [6], aspect [6], slope [4], viewshed [4], roughness, tpi, tri [1-3 each] / - rasterize [7], pixel-info [7], calc [7], mosaic [6] + stack, tile [5], footprint [5]"
72	
73	followed by **[verbatim]**: *"The directive tells the implementer where the candidate is weak without giving away the sample."*
74	
75	### 1.3 The numbers that are actually on the page
76	
77	Headline `gdal` pair **[verbatim]**: *"It wrote 17,000 lines of C++ and reproduced 36 percent of the program's behavior... It did not run out of time or budget. It stopped because, by its own assessment, it was done."* and *"This run grew to 115,000 lines and reached 90 percent behavioral parity."* Method notes say **[verbatim]** *"The gdal, 7-Zip, and DuckDB numbers in the opening section are Fable 5 runs."*
78	
79	Other headline pairs **[verbatim]**: *"the same system took its 7-Zip recreation from 54 percent parity to 95 percent and its DuckDB recreation from 34 to 80 percent."*
80	
81	The *frontier* figure ("best single agent vs best system, per task") is server-rendered and carries all 24 task pairs in its SVG tooltips. Extracted in full:
82	
83	| task | single-agent frontier | system frontier | delta |
84	|---|---|---|---|
85	| ffmpeg | 10.7 | 40.3 | +29.6 |
86	| gromacs | 15.1 | 30.6 | +15.6 |
87	| ctags | 28.4 | 76.4 | +48.0 |
88	| cppcheck | 30.3 | 54.2 | +23.9 |
89	| duckdb | 34.2 | 80.0 | +45.9 |
90	| doxygen | 37.5 | 60.7 | +23.2 |
91	| pandoc | 39.5 | 84.2 | +44.7 |
92	| lnav | 43.5 | 83.9 | +40.4 |
93	| ast-grep | 58.0 | 86.8 | +28.7 |
94	| gdal | 58.5 | 90.3 | +31.8 |
95	| tree-sitter | 61.9 | 90.9 | +29.1 |
96	| samtools | 62.1 | 96.5 | +34.4 |
97	| typst | 67.2 | 78.0 | +10.8 |
98	| delta | 68.0 | 91.4 | +23.4 |
99	| lazygit | 69.6 | 93.2 | +23.6 |
100	| sox | 70.5 | 99.5 | +29.0 |
101	| bedtools2 | 75.2 | 98.2 | +23.0 |
102	| scc | 78.0 | 88.4 | +10.3 |
103	| 7zip | 78.2 | 94.9 | +16.7 |
104	| svgbob | 83.3 | 93.4 | +10.2 |
105	| solar | 87.0 | 89.9 | +2.9 |
106	| peco | 92.4 | 99.6 | +7.2 |
107	| stgit | 93.3 | 96.9 | +3.6 |
108	| proj | 97.3 | 99.4 | +2.1 |
109	
110	**My computation from that table (inference, not a Factory claim):** median single-agent frontier **64.65**, median system frontier **90.10**; mean 59.99 → 83.23; median delta **+23.50**, mean +23.25, range +2.1 to +48.0; **zero regressions** at the frontier level; median fraction of the remaining gap closed **70.6 %**, mean 63.5 %.
111	
112	Note the frontier is best-of-three-models per task per condition, so `gdal` reads 58.5 → 90.3 here while the Fable-only headline reads 36 → 90.
113	
114	Cost **[verbatim]**: *"The system runs were far longer and more expensive; for gdal, 14 times the credits and 13 times the wall time. But budget was not what separated the conditions. Every single-agent campaign ended because the agent decided to end it. Additional compute does not help an agent that will not spend it."*
115	
116	### 1.4 What the article itself says about its limits — this is unusually honest and should be read as such
117	
118	Method notes, all **[verbatim]**:
119	
120	- *"One run per cell. Every number here is a single run. Nothing was repeated to average it, so no cell carries a variance estimate, and none of these figures should be read as a mean."*
121	- *"Coverage. 141 of the 144 cells have been graded. The remaining three system runs - gdal and gromacs on Sol, samtools on Kimi - were interrupted and not rerun before publication; they carry no score."*
122	- *"Opus substitutes. Six cells in the Fable panel are Opus runs standing in for Fable ones that were safety-blocked, either in the single-agent or system run: bedtools2, gromacs, pandoc, samtools, sox and tree-sitter."*
123	- *"The campaigns were not compute-matched; each continued until the single agent or system orchestrator decided to ship."*
124	- *"We selected 24 of the benchmark's hardest tasks, based on the current top leaderboard score. The set was hand-picked, weighted toward low best-public scores. Some hard-end candidates (php-src, pueue, ditaa, quickjs, chroma, miller) were dropped during screening for persistent safety blocks, single-agent saturation, or a score gated by one undocumented environment variable."*
125	
126	So: n=1 per cell, no variance, a hand-picked hard subset with screened-out candidates, unmatched compute, three ungraded cells, six substituted cells. The effect size is large enough that noise is unlikely to explain it, but no confidence interval exists and none is claimed.
127	
128	### 1.5 ProgramBench is third-party, and the metric matters (independent)
129	
130	ProgramBench is **not** Factory's benchmark. "ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch?", arXiv:2605.03546v1, 2026-05-05, led by John Yang and Kilian Lieret (Meta FAIR) with Harvard and Stanford collaborators. 200 tasks, mostly Rust/Go/C/C++, 248,853 test functions total (median 770 per task). The reference is execute-only, internet blocked, tests never revealed.
131	
132	**The paper's own primary metric is not the one Factory reports.** From the paper: *"% Resolved is the primary metric: the fraction of 200 tasks where all tests pass"*, with *"% Almost"* relaxing to ≥95 % passing. Its baselines: **no model fully resolved any task**; the best (Claude Opus 4.7) reached ≥95 % pass on 3 % of tasks, 0 % fully resolved.
133	
134	Factory reports *behavioral parity* — the raw fraction of hidden-suite checks passed, pinned at `pb-1.2.0` — which corresponds to the paper's *Raw Pass Rate*, not *% Resolved*. Factory never claims to resolve tasks, and says so precisely: **[verbatim]** *"Every score is the official metric from the hidden suite, pinned at pb-1.2.0 and computed identically for single-agent and system artifacts."* The distinction is load-bearing for anyone repeating these numbers.
135	
136	Independent leaderboard context (Vals AI, ProgramBench, retrieved 2026-09-06, scores dated 2026-09-04, run under a *mini-SWE-agent harness*): GPT-6 Astra 85.4 % raw pass / 11 fully resolved; Claude Fable 5.1 82.7 % / 14; Claude Opus 5 82.3 % / 6 — over all 200 tasks. Factory's system-condition median of 90.1 is on the hardest 24 with a much stronger harness, so it is a genuinely strong result and simultaneously not comparable to those rows.
137	
138	There is also a live methodological dispute: "Is ProgramBench Impossible?" argues some tasks test undocumented behavior reachable through no observable channel (the cited example is `seqtk`'s undocumented `hrum` and `kfreq` sub-commands); ProgramBench's authors reply that every test asserts observable deterministic behavior of a binary the model may run freely, so tasks are solvable by construction through probing. Factory's design — a validator that probes the oracle and weights cases — is a direct response to that difficulty, whichever way the dispute settles.
139	
140	---
141	
142	## 2. Source inventory
143	
144	All Factory sources are primary. Dates are each page's own `datePublished`.
145	
146	| id | title | date | type |
147	|---|---|---|---|
148	| `factory-large-tasks` | What it Takes for Coding Agents to Complete Large Software Tasks | 2026-08-27 | primary |
149	| `factory-missions-arch` | How Missions Work | 2026-04-10 | primary |
150	| `factory-missions` | Missions | 2025-02-26 | primary |
151	| `factory-context-window` | The Context Window Problem: Scaling Agents Beyond Token Limits | 2025-08-25 | primary |
152	| `factory-compressing-context` | Compressing Context | 2025-07-21 | primary |
153	| `factory-evaluating-compression` | Evaluating Compression | 2025-12-16 | primary |
154	| `factory-deferred-context` | Deferred Context Engine | 2026-05-20 | primary |
155	| `factory-terminal-bench` | Droid: the #1 Software Development Agent on Terminal-Bench | 2025-09-25 | primary |
156	| `factory-legacy-bench` | Legacy-Bench: Can AI Agents Maintain the World's Most Critical Software? | 2026-04-01 | primary |
157	| `factory-model-routing` | Model Routing Belongs in the Harness | 2026-08-24 | primary |
158	| `factory-agent-effectiveness` | Agent Effectiveness | 2026-08-13 | primary |
159	| `factory-docs-autonomy` | Autonomy Level (docs) | retrieved 2026-09-06 | primary |
160	| `factory-docs-spec-mode` | Interaction Modes / Spec Mode (docs) | retrieved 2026-09-06 | primary |
161	| `factory-docs-droid-exec` | Droid Exec (Headless) (docs) | retrieved 2026-09-06 | primary |
162	| `factory-docs-subagents` | Custom droids (subagents) (docs) | retrieved 2026-09-06 | primary |
163	| `factory-docs-droid-shield` | Droid Shield (docs) | retrieved 2026-09-06 | primary |
164	| `factory-docs-cli` | Droid CLI Overview (docs) | retrieved 2026-09-06 | primary |
165	| `programbench-paper` | ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch? (arXiv:2605.03546) | 2026-05-05 | independent |
166	| `vals-programbench` | Vals AI ProgramBench leaderboard | scores 2026-09-04 | independent |
167	| `llmstats-tb2` | llm-stats Terminal-Bench 2.0 leaderboard | updated 2026-09-06 | independent |
168	| `lw-programbench` | Is ProgramBench Impossible? (LessWrong) + ProgramBench reply | 2026 | independent |
169	
170	Notable third-party number: llm-stats' Terminal-Bench 2.0 board (2026-09-06) lists **models**, not agents — GPT-5.5 0.827, Claude Mythos Preview 0.820, Claude Sonnet 5 0.804 — and carries **no Factory Droid row**. A secondary aggregator reports "Factory Droid + GPT-5.3-Codex 77.3 %" on TB2; I could not confirm that on a primary leaderboard, so it should not be repeated as fact. Factory's own 2025-09-25 Terminal-Bench post (58.75 % on Core v0.1.1) is a Factory claim about an older benchmark version and is not comparable to TB2 rows.
171	
172	---
173	
174	## 3. Mechanism inventory
175	
176	For each: what it does, the evidence, and the limits or silences.
177	
178	### M1 — An independent completion standard authored before implementation
179	**Does:** a validator builds an executable "instrument" — a weighted inventory of behavioral cases plus comparison rules — before the implementer writes anything, and the implementation is held to it.
180	**Evidence:** the whole primary article; the `gdal` grading policy quoted above; the claimed effect is the article's entire result (median +23.5 points at the frontier by my computation).
181	**Limits / silences:** ProgramBench supplies an oracle binary, which is what makes an instrument constructible. Factory says so **[verbatim]**: *"ProgramBench gave that standard a particular shape: an inventory and weighted sample recovered from a black-box reference. Other tasks draw their standard from different sources."* How the instrument is built when there is no oracle — a greenfield product feature — is asserted, not demonstrated. There is no reported measure of instrument *quality* independent of the hidden suite, and no ablation isolating the instrument from the other two roles.
182	
183	### M2 — Role separation: orchestrator / implementer / validator
184	**Does:** three roles with one goal each. Orchestrator plans, adjudicates findings, issues directives, decides when to ship. Implementer builds. Validator measures.
185	**Evidence:** primary article; `factory-missions-arch` gives the rationale **[verbatim]**: *"An agent's trajectory is append-only, so the model's reasoning at any given point is a function of every past thought, observation, and action"* and *"An agent that implemented something is worse at objectively evaluating its own work than a fresh, unbiased reviewer. Its prior reasoning creates a bias toward confirming what it already did."*
186	**Limits:** in the ProgramBench experiment **[verbatim]** *"Within each non-substituted model panel, the single agent and all three system roles used the same model at the same reasoning level"* — so role separation is context separation, not model diversity, in that experiment. In production the default differs: `factory-model-routing` says **[verbatim]** *"our default validator comes from a different model family than our default implementer."* No ablation separates the orchestrator's contribution from the validator's.
187	
188	### M3 — The wall (information barrier around the sample)
189	**Does:** the implementer never authors, runs, or sees the instrument's cases or raw output; only clustered, feature-level directives cross. The validator may expand the instrument but not weaken it to fit the candidate.
190	**Evidence:** the *wall* quotes above; the published directive showing weights and area names without cases.
191	**Limits / silences:** **the sources describe the wall as an architectural property and never describe an enforcement mechanism.** Where the instrument's files live relative to the implementer's workspace, whether the implementer has a shell that could read them, and what happens if it does, are all unstated. There is no described detection of a candidate that edits check-owned files, and no tamper verdict. The one-directional rule ("cannot weaken or revise it to accommodate the candidate") is stated as a rule, with no described gate that refuses a weakening edit.
192	
193	### M4 — Validation contract before features (Missions)
194	**Does:** at mission level the orchestrator writes a validation contract — a finite checklist of testable behavioral assertions — *before* decomposing into features; each feature then claims which assertions it fulfils; features group into milestones.
195	**Evidence:** `factory-missions-arch` **[verbatim]**: *"the orchestrator defines correctness first - creating a validation contract, a set of behavioral assertions that define success, before defining any features. This ordering matters. When creating the validation contract, the orchestrator draws from its understanding of requirements. If it had created the features first, the contract would be influenced by the implementation it had already planned."*
196	**Limits:** the contract is authored by the same orchestrator that later adjudicates. Assertions are natural-language plus evidence hints (`Evidence: screenshot, network(POST /api/auth/login -> 200)`), not executable checks. Nothing described prevents the orchestrator from reinterpreting an assertion at validation time.
197	
198	### M5 — Test-driven development at two levels
199	**Does:** each worker writes tests before code; separately, black-box "user-testing validators" exercise the finished system the way a user would, against the validation contract.
200	**Evidence:** `factory-missions-arch` **[verbatim]**: *"Each worker writes tests before code, so the tests reflect intended behavior rather than implementation details"* and *"These assertions are later verified by fresh agents that exercise the system as a black box - using it the way a real user would - rather than inspecting the code that implements them."*
201	**Limits:** worker-authored tests are inside the same context that wrote the code, which is the exact failure M1 exists to fix; the black-box validators are the compensating layer. No number is given for how often black-box validation catches what worker tests missed.
202	
203	### M6 — Fresh context per unit of work
204	**Does:** every feature gets a worker starting from a fresh context with only its feature spec; validators are fresh agents; state lives in shared artifacts.
205	**Evidence:** `factory-missions-arch` **[verbatim]**: *"A programmatic runner takes the feature list and spawns a worker for each feature in order. Each worker starts with a fresh context, receives its feature spec, writes tests first, then implements."* and *"No single agent needs to hold the complete picture in its context at once. The full state is distributed across shared artifacts: the validation contract, the feature list, research notes, operational guidelines, and an evolving knowledge base."*
206	**Limits:** the runner is described as sequential (*"spawns a worker for each feature in order"*). No durable-resume story is described; what happens to an interrupted mission is unstated.
207	
208	### M7 — Anchored iterative summarization (compaction)
209	**Does:** a persistent structured summary with explicit sections (session intent, file modifications, decisions, next steps); on compression only the newly truncated span is summarized and merged into the persisted summary, rather than regenerating the whole thing.
210	**Evidence:** `factory-compressing-context` names the two thresholds (a "fill line" and a "drain line") and the four failure modes of naive re-summarization — redundant re-summarization, linear cost growth, forced hierarchical summarization, and **[verbatim]** *"Perpetual edge-of-limit: once we start summarizing, we run permanently near max context, which empirically degrades response quality."* The framing target is **[verbatim]** *"Our aim is to minimize tokens per task, not per request."*
211	**Limits:** the thresholds are described as a tradeoff to be tuned per task shape; no defaults are published.
212	
213	### M8 — Probe-based evaluation of compression
214	**Does:** rather than ROUGE or embedding similarity, after compression the agent is asked probe questions (recall, artifact, continuation, decision) that require the truncated detail; an LLM judge (GPT-5.2) scores six dimensions.
215	**Evidence:** `factory-evaluating-compression`, over **[verbatim]** *"more than 36,000 messages from production sessions"* (methodology section says 36,611) from users on an opt-in research program. Reported: Factory +0.35 over OpenAI and +0.26 over Anthropic overall; technical accuracy 4.04 / 3.74 / 3.43; continuation 4.01 vs Anthropic 3.56; compression ratios 98.6 % / 98.7 % / 99.3 %. **[verbatim]**: *"Factory retains about 0.7% more tokens than OpenAI, but gains 0.35 quality points."*
216	**Limits, stated by Factory [verbatim]:** *"Artifact tracking remains an unsolved problem. All methods scored between 2.19 and 2.45 out of 5.0 on knowing which files were created, modified, or examined."* Also: self-run evaluation of one's own product against competitors, LLM-judge scoring, Factory summaries came from production while the comparators were generated by calling their APIs on the same prefixes — a plausible asymmetry Factory does not quantify.
217	
218	### M9 — Deferred context engine (progressive disclosure of capabilities)
219	**Does:** internal tool schemas, MCP tool schemas, skills, and plugin instructions are not in the prompt; a compact capability index (names, short descriptions, server names, input hints) is, and full schemas load on demand through a loader tool, then stay warm.
220	**Evidence:** `factory-deferred-context` **[verbatim]**: *"On each turn, Droid keeps a compact capability index: tool names, short descriptions, server names, and enough input hints to decide whether a capability is relevant. Full schemas and long-form instructions stay deferred until Droid calls a loader, promotes the capability, and keeps it available for the rest of the work."* Production telemetry over five days, bucketed by hidden deferred tool count: **21.0 %** average estimated input-token reduction at 20–50 hidden tools, **50.8 %** at 100+; roughly 15 % average across MCP-triggered enterprise sessions.
221	**Limits, partly stated by Factory:** the savings are *estimated* input tokens against a hypothetical "everything loaded" baseline, not measured against a real control arm. Factory explicitly declines the all-turns aggregate as a headline **[verbatim]**: *"The all-turns aggregate is intentionally not the headline: it includes small sessions, empty deferred catalogs, and reminder overhead."* No task-success measurement accompanies the token saving — the claim is cost/latency, not quality.
222	
223	### M10 — Memory across sessions

334	## 5. (a) Where Factory is genuinely ahead today, and what it would take to match
335	
336	Ranked by how much the gap costs us.
337	
338	1. **A validator that derives the standard from a reference.** This is the single mechanism their data supports, and we do not have it: our standards are transcribed from pre-declared environment checks. To match: a `validator`-role preset with a check-authoring tool over `ctx.completionStandards`, plus a comparator vocabulary on `StandardCheck` rich enough to express their four-channel byte comparison and *named, licensed normalizers* — a relaxation that must carry evidence, which `relax()` already models. Concretely: extend `StandardCheck` with `comparator` and `normalizers[]`, ship `dsh-tool-standard-author` restricted to `validator` role, and prove `standard_authored_before_first_write` in `SessionFacts`.
339	
340	2. **A shipped multi-goal program runner.** Missions decomposes into features and milestones, spawns a worker per feature, runs validation rounds, and generates fix features (their published mission: six milestones, 38.8k lines with 52.5 % tests, 89.25 % statement coverage, 81 issues surfaced, 21 fix features, 2–4 validation rounds per milestone, median 51 assistant turns per implementation run). We have `tool-ralph` (sequential, one objective) and a `proposed` `ProgramLedger`. To match: `@deepseek-ai/dsh-program` with durable `program/*` events mapping each goal to its session, workspace, preset, isolation, budget, and status, and an integration goal whose standard runs against the merged head.
341	
342	3. **Failure clustering into feature-level directives.** Their validator *"groups failures by root cause"* and the orchestrator turns those into a directive naming missing features with weights but no cases. Our runner issues one directive whose `rootCause` is a count of failing checks and whose `detail` is bounded raw evidence. To match: a directive-clustering consumer between `verification/run` and the `<validation_failed>` block, keeping the no-case-leak property we already have.
343	
344	4. **Deferred tool and MCP schemas.** Measured 21 %–50.8 % input-token reduction at large catalogs. We defer skills and load every tool schema. To match: a capability-index projection over `ctx.tools.schemas(agent)` plus a promote-on-demand loader, with the KV-cache consequence stated in the Model Experience section (promotion changes the prefix, so it must be turn-aligned).
345	
346	5. **Cache-aware model routing in the harness.** Their analysis — cache-blind switching reaching 2.12–2.37× an all-frontier baseline while cache-aware routing stays at 0.19–0.28× — is a design we can implement directly against `usage/priced` and the cache token fields we already fold. To match: a router plugin on `agent/pre-step` that prices staying-warm against switching, with every decision a durable event.
347	
348	6. **A graded autonomy ladder with risk-classified operations and org enforcement**, and the enterprise surface behind it (SSO, enforced settings, secret gate, issue attribution).
349	
350	7. **Published, dated results on a public benchmark.** They have Terminal-Bench, ProgramBench, Legacy-Bench, and a compression evaluation. We have zero public numbers. This is a distribution gap, not an engineering one, but it is the one a client notices first.

352	## 5. (b) Where our design is stronger by construction, and the evidence each claim needs
353	
354	For each: the claim, why it holds in code today, and the **public artefact** that would make it verifiable rather than asserted.
355	
356	1. **The session log is the sole authority.** Every model-visible input is reconstructable from the log; `dsh-verification` rebuilds its whole view from events; the budget policy measures from the log rather than memory precisely so a breach is reproducible by anyone holding it.
357	   *Evidence needed:* publish a persisted log plus the fold that regenerates every number we quote from it, and let a third party rerun `pnpm run test:snapshot` keylessly and get byte-identical transcripts.
358	
359	2. **Certificates carry their executor and isolation, and cannot be forged past replay.** `recordRun()` refuses `process`/`host` for an `agent-reported` run; the `./invariant` companion rejects a certificate with no fully passing run of the same standard revision, one whose executor differs from the run it cites, and one whose census carries a denied tool authority.
360	   *Evidence needed:* a published hand-authored log carrying a forged certificate together with the invariant's refusal, and a published run where an `agent-reported` executor is visibly capped at `none`.
361	
362	3. **The read barrier is filesystem and process authority, not a promise.** Denial happens in the operation that opens paths, the tool guard is monotonic, and the composition census is durable and cross-checked against every `request/header`'s tool names.
363	   *Evidence needed:* the `read-barrier-denied` keyless snapshot, **plus an honest red-team demonstration that a shell-capable implementer does reach the standard today and does not after slice 5.** Publishing the second half without the first would repeat the exact overstatement our own council review caught.
364	
365	4. **Usage is priced as durable evidence with a pricing-table digest.** `usage/priced` carries the rates that priced it, so cost replays without the config, and a changed table changes the digest.
366	   *Evidence needed:* a fixture proving the same log prices identically under the same digest and refuses to pool under a different one, and a published cost-per-certified-session that names its digest.
367	
368	5. **Experiments are frozen before results are visible and reproduce byte-identically.** The plan digest is always recomputed from content, a declared digest that disagrees is `EXPERIMENT_PLAN_NOT_FROZEN`, and the bootstrap seed derives from the digest.
369	   *Evidence needed:* publish a plan digest, both arms' session ids, and the interval — then let someone recompute the interval from the logs and get the same bytes.
370	
371	6. **Composition is content-addressed and quarantinable.** Content digests and `componentAddress()` have landed in `dsh-components`; the `composition/manifest` event and the quarantine consumers have not.
372	   *Evidence needed:* land the manifest, then publish two runs on different hosts under different `DSH_HOME` values with identical `compositionSha256`, and one run where a `tool-cordis` mount flips `dynamicPackagesMounted` and the export counts the session `quarantined`.
373	
374	7. **Held-out decontamination keys on content hashes, and export withholds by default.** `environment/run` carries prompt/fixture/checks hashes and a combined key; `dsh-trajectories` withholds held-out sessions unless explicitly asked, and withholds configured districts.
375	   *Evidence needed:* publish a `TrajectoryExportReport` showing `heldOut`, `withheld`, `filtered`, and `skipped` counts that sum to the input.
376	
377	8. **RL data export exists and its reward comes from a certificate.** `dsh-trajectory/1` lines carry the environment stamp and a reward a certificate decided.
378	   *Evidence needed:* publish the format, one rewarded line, and the certificate it traces to — and the tamper fixture that yields `outcome: 0`, which requires slice 6.
379	
380	9. **Every package documents its token and KV-cache effect.** This is already checkable in-repo and has no public counterpart.
381	   *Evidence needed:* none beyond making the repository public; it is self-evidencing.

395	## 5. (d) Claims never to make without evidence
396	
397	1. **Never** say our checks are hidden, or that a certificate proves the implementer could not see the standard, until read-barrier slice 5 has landed and the census shows `denied-at-executor` for shell, subprocess, and terminal. Today a shell-capable implementer reads the standard.
398	2. **Never** publish a certificate rate before tamper verdicts exist. Until slice 6, every public row must carry `tamper: not instrumented`, and those rates must feed neither the archive's quality term nor a training reward.
399	3. **Never** claim an isolation level above `none` for a run whose session log does not carry the census and, for `host`, the verified attestation. `none` asserts nothing, and saying otherwise is the one claim that would destroy the value of every other number we publish.
400	4. **Never** state a cost or a cost-per-certified-session before `usage/priced` is folded, and never state one without naming its pricing-table digest.
401	5. **Never** name a competitor's model or agent in a comparison before that route pair shares an `ExperimentResult` verdict under one preset and one isolation, with the composition digest stamped. For a commercial lab this is a substantiation exposure as well as a methodological one.
402	6. **Never** average or rank across `isolation` or the held-out split; both stay columns a reader partitions by, and the fleet leaderboard already refuses to blend them.
403	7. **Never** report a certificate rate computed from surviving rows alone. A session that is skipped, torn by a restart, or interrupted must appear as an error row; a missing row inflates every rate computed from the rest.
404	8. **Never** repeat a benchmark number without its metric, its harness, its task subset, and its repetition count. Specifically: *behavioral parity / raw pass rate is not % Resolved*, and quoting Factory's 90 % beside ProgramBench's "no model fully resolved any task" without that distinction is a misrepresentation of both.
405	9. **Never** claim a per-run improvement from a single run per cell — ours or anyone's — without an interval. `dsh-experiments` exists so we never have to.
406	10. **Never** claim a skill, prompt section, or preset improved anything without paired present-versus-absent cells; a plausible mechanism and a happy transcript are not evidence.
407	11. **Never** claim training data is decontaminated without pointing at the `environment/run` content hashes the check keys on, and never claim a transcript is exportable without a redaction profile and pinned data-use terms.
408	12. **Never** describe a harness-versus-model result without pinning the harness variant. A checkpoint measured on a harness that co-evolved with it measures the pair.
409	13. **Never** cite a number produced by a summarizing tool without checking it against the source. This document contains a worked example of that failure: four per-model medians and a "73 % gap closed" figure that exist nowhere in Factory's page.
