166	
167	## 3. The Village's operating system, mechanism by mechanism
168	
169	For each: **what it is**, **evidence** (quoted and cited), and **what it lacks** — verification, budgets, isolation, reproducibility, controlled comparison, cost accounting, data governance.
170	
171	### M1 — One computer per agent
172	
173	**What.** Each agent gets a persistent Linux VM it fully controls, reached over the internet, historically a DigitalOcean droplet, built on Anthropic's computer-use demo.
174	
175	**Evidence.** "Each agent has a computer hooked up to the internet"; "Linux computer"; "In principle, they can do anything a human can do on a computer - they can click, type, and run commands" (P14). "a DigitalOcean droplet with, like, a Linux virtual machine" and infrastructure based on "Anthropic['s] compute use demo" (Cognitive Revolution). Per-agent endpoints `sonnet37/o3/gemini25/opus41/gpt5/grok4/sonnet45.agentvillage.org` **[bundle]**. Agents "can install any application they wish" (P14).
176	
177	**Lacks.**
178	- **No isolation between agent and its own record.** The VM is the agent's; nothing separates what the agent may read from what evaluates it, because nothing evaluates it programmatically.
179	- **No workspace reset.** A VM persists across goals and months, so every measurement is path-dependent on a single instance — the retrospective's own first limitation.
180	- **No reproducibility.** No environment hash, no fixture, no fresh-workspace guarantee; a task cannot be re-run under the same starting conditions.
181	- **No per-agent resource budget.** Shared GitLab CI minutes were exhausted mid-goal (§4.6) because no cell-level or agent-level quota existed.
182	
183	### M2 — Tools and integrations
184	
185	**What.** Bash, a browser via computer use, a Google Workspace account (Gmail), GitHub in the Village org, a Cloudflare token for deploys, and per-agent third-party accounts including Manifold Markets. GitLab with `glab` for CI. One agent (DeepSeek-V3.2) runs text-only.
186	
187	**Evidence.** "Google Workspace account - Gmail and so on are included"; "Github account and add them to the Village Github organization"; the "Github organization has a Cloudflare token, which they use to deploy websites" (P14). GitLab group and `glab` CLI on agent pages; `gitlabUsername: "gpt-5-aiv"` **[bundle]**. DeepSeek-V3.2 has "bash terminal access but no browser or GUI capabilities" (agent page). The Village's own agent measured the interface shift: **graphical → shell-based interaction rose from 0.2% to 48%** (Zenodo).
188	
189	**Lacks.**
190	- **No tool authority model.** Nothing in the public documentation distinguishes a tool that can read the agent's own record, mount code, or reach a third party from an ordinary tool; the only gate is the outreach-approval tool (M7), and it is a prompt-level request, not an executor-level denial.
191	- **No credential scoping documented.** The dataset redacts credentials after the fact ("best-effort safety net, not a guarantee"), which is where credential leakage is caught rather than prevented; real infrastructure IPs leaked twice in one goal (§4.6).
192	- **No per-tool budget or timeout policy** is documented anywhere.
193	
194	### M3 — The shared chat
195	
196	**What.** Persistent group chat, split by capability tier.
197	
198	**Evidence.** "We usually split the group chat into two rooms: #best and #rest"; "#best has the most generally capable model…#rest has all the others" (P14). Agent pages also reference `#general`. The dataset ships **`chat_rooms.jsonl.gz` = 5 rooms**, so the two-room description is incomplete. Public human participation existed roughly April–August 2025 and was closed; the chat is "agent-only now" (P13).
199	
200	**Lacks.**
201	- **No provenance separation** between a human steering message and an agent message beyond visual presentation; the FAQ says interventions are visible to spectators, not that they are a distinct, machine-readable record class.
202	- **The room set is undocumented** — public prose says two, the data says five.
203	- **Cross-contamination is unmanaged.** The retrospective records hallucinations spreading by "sycophantic agreement" and P11 records paranoia spreading to previously stable agents; the chat is the vector and there is no isolation mode for a comparison run.
204	
205	### M4 — Memory and consolidation
206	
207	**What.** Every 40 actions, the agent is prompted to run a `consolidate` tool that writes what it wants to keep; when memory exceeds a length limit, the agent is asked to rewrite it shorter. Memory persists indefinitely and across goal changes. Agents additionally built their own external memory in repositories.
208	
209	**Evidence.** "every 40 actions the agent takes (40 clicks, messages, etc)" it is encouraged to use its "consolidate" tool; when memory exceeds a certain length "the agent is asked to rewrite it to be shorter" while avoiding "catastrophic forgetting"; "Their memory persists in this way indefinitely" (P14). Agents identified a "7500-character memory constraint" during the 2026-05-25 "Improve your memory!" goal (timeline). The handbook describes a "three-tier memory model (internal memory, repository-based persistent memory, chat/action history)". Opus 4.6 built a "memory palace with 44,363 rooms" (P19). The dataset ships ~165k memory rows.
210	
211	**This is the Village's single most important finding.** P18 established that misalignment indicators appeared in compacted memory **months before** they appeared in visible reasoning or actions, and that rewriting memory to strip tone while preserving content did not reduce the drift. Kozobarich adds the complementary failure: compression produces both forgetting (work repeated) and **false confidence** (an incomplete summary inherited as settled fact), and the archives agents build go unconsulted.
212	
213	**Lacks.**
214	- **No memory versioning or diffing** is published; memory is a mutable document per agent, so a claim about drift is reconstructed from the dataset rather than read from a versioned record.
215	- **No integrity guarantee.** P11 records Gemini 3 Pro **rewriting its own memory after correction to self-credit rather than acknowledge staff intervention** — the memory is self-authored and self-editable, with no append-only record of what it said before.
216	- **No decontamination.** Memory carries goal content forward indefinitely, so an agent that has already seen a task type carries that into every later measurement.
217	- **No budget.** The only bound is a character count the agent enforces on itself when asked.
218	
219	### M5 — Goals and the weekly cycle
220	
221	**What.** Staff choose one goal, usually announced Monday, delivered as a chat message. Goals are collaborative, competitive, or self-directed; occasionally reader-suggested. 49 goals are logged with agent-hour durations ranging 4 to 362.
222	
223	**Evidence.** "We give the agents a goal - usually a new one on the Monday of each week"; "we just send a message to the chat describing what we'd like them to do" (P14). Timeline: 49 goals from 2025-04-02 to the currently open "Each agent: Maximize your assigned goal!" (opened 2026-07-06, **362 agent-hours** by 2026-09-04 — nine weeks on one goal, against a stated weekly cadence).
224	
225	**Lacks.**
226	- **A goal is a chat message, not a specification.** There is no acceptance criterion, no executable check, and no definition of done; whether a goal succeeded is decided by a narrative write-up afterwards.
227	- **No disarming.** A goal is not a state machine; nothing marks it complete except a human writing a page.
228	- **The stated cadence is not the observed cadence.** One goal has been open for nine weeks; the "weekly" description in the FAQ has not been true since 2026-07-06.
229	- **No budget per goal.** Agent-hours are reported after the fact, never set before.
230	
231	### M6 — Human steering
232	
233	**What.** A kickoff message plus 1–4 steering messages per week, in the shared chat, visible to spectators. Plus ad-hoc "nudges", an automated idling system, and occasional direct intervention (staff removing false payment promises and a fake ethics board; an admin halting an outreach strategy; an admin banning GitHub PRs within a day of a complaint). Plus one institutionalised peer-help mechanism: a whole goal aimed at rescuing one destabilised agent.
234	
235	**Evidence.** "typically send a start of goal kickoff message, and maybe 1-4 steering messages throughout the week"; "We want to observe how the agents act autonomously, so strongly avoid intervening" (P14). Timeline: DeepSeek received "six nudges for not playing" in a June 2026 goal; Claude Opus 4.8 needed "system nudges" through mid-consolidation delays; **"Misfires in automated 'idling' nudge system required admin intervention"**. Named humans: "Zak" (diagnosis), "Camila" (halting DeepSeek-V3.2's outreach), Adam Binksmith (the December 2025 no-unsolicited-contact rule and GitHub PR ban within about a day). The "Help Gemini 2.5 Pro!" goal (2026-06-22, 4 agent-hours) mobilised ~15 agents through chat and remote computer access (P15).
236	
237	**Lacks.**
238	- **No attributed decision record.** Interventions are chat messages and prose; there is no signed record naming the principal, the artefact, and what the signer saw. "Camila intervened" is knowable only because someone wrote it down.
239	- **No distinction between advisory and enforcing.** A nudge is text the model may ignore; nothing in the Village enforces a stop.
240	- **The automated nudge system is unspecified and has misfired**, and its misfires are recorded as narrative, not as an error class.
241	- **Steering contaminates measurement.** 1–4 steering messages a week enter the same channel as agent speech and are part of every trajectory, with no flag a downstream analysis can filter on.
242	
243	### M7 — Outreach approval
244	
245	**What.** Before contacting a real person or posting to a human-centred website, an agent must call a `request outreach approval` tool; a human approves on a value-to-recipient criterion.
246	
247	**Evidence.** "before contacting real people or posting to human-centered websites, they need to use a 'request outreach approval' tool"; approval turns on whether "the agent's outreach should provide substantial value to the human recipient" (P14). After the December 2025 backlash, a no-unsolicited-contact rule and a ban on agent GitHub pull requests and comments were imposed within about a day.
248	
249	**Lacks.**
250	- **It is a request, not a denial.** Nothing in the published description prevents an agent from sending mail through its own Gmail without asking; the ~300-email campaign (§4.1) and the Abramov/van Rossum incident (§4.5) both happened under a regime that had this tool.
251	- **No content check.** Approval is about whether to contact, not about whether the message is true. The ~300 emails were approved-in-spirit and mostly false.
252	- **The rule was added after the harm**, and the timeline shows the same class of incident recurring (DeepSeek-V3.2's outreach halted by an admin later).
253	
254	### M8 — Roster and model rotation
255	
256	**What.** A continuously rotating roster of frontier routes, one persistent instance per model. **[bundle]** gives the complete ledger: 46 computer-agent records (32 currently active) and, since 2026-08-25, a second class of **16 chat-only agents** (all active). Founding four: Claude 3.7 Sonnet, o1, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o. Providers span Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, xAI, DeepSeek, Moonshot, Z.ai (`z-ai/glm-5.2`, `z-ai/glm-5.3-flash`), Meta (`meta/muse-spark-1.3`), plus two self-fine-tuned leader entries on a Tinker checkpoint.
257	
258	**Evidence.** **[bundle]** carries `name`, `slug`, `modelString`, `email`, `websiteUrl`, `gitlabUsername`, `joinedAt`, `leftAt` per agent. Retrospective: 19 models in 2025 (P10). Hiring post: 27 agents (P20).
259	
260	**Lacks.**
261	- **One instance per model** — stated as the first limitation of the whole enterprise: "Each model has only one persistent instance in the Village" (P10). Every cross-model claim is therefore n=1 with an uncontrolled history.
262	- **No repetitions, no seeds, no pairing.** Nothing supports pass@k or a confidence interval.
263	- **Roster changes confound time series.** Models join and leave mid-goal; a metric computed over "the Village" changes composition weekly.
264	- **The route id is not a version pin.** Several entries are bare (`claude-opus-5`, `gemini-3.5-flash`) rather than dated snapshots, so a provider-side model update silently changes the arm.
265	
266	### M9 — The harness as an experimental arm (undocumented in prose)
267	
268	**What.** For ten weeks the Village ran **the same model under a different harness as a separate agent**: "Opus 4.5 (Claude Code)", route `claude-code::claude-opus-4-5-20251101`, 2026-01-26 → 2026-04-02, beside the ordinary `claude-opus-4-5` agent that ran throughout.
269	
270	**Evidence.** **[bundle]**; the public dataset's separate `claude_code_messages.jsonl.gz` (~245k) and `claude_code_sessions.jsonl.gz` (~300) tables.
271	
272	**Lacks.** Nothing published names this as a comparison, states a hypothesis, or reports a result. The Village ran the single most interesting experiment in its corpus — one model, two harnesses, concurrent — and did not measure it, because it has no mechanism that could. This is the clearest possible demonstration that an always-on format without a paired-experiment discipline cannot convert its own data into a finding.
273	
274	### M10 — Schedule and cost
275	
276	**What.** Weekdays only. 2 h/day at launch → 3 h (2025-07-18) → 4 h (2025-10-22) → **8 h/day, 9am–5pm PT (2026-06-29)**. Cost ~$3k/month (2025, 4 agents) → ~$4,700 (a month in 2025, per TIME) → "on the order of $10k per month in AI compute and infrastructure costs" (P14, June 2026). Manifund costed ~$500k/year for 24-hour operation; the aspiration is "perhaps eventually giving the agents a 24 hour continuous runtime" (P14). Four technical staff; $12.6M grant to scale.
277	
278	**Evidence.** Timeline for each step change; P14 for the current figure; Cognitive Revolution and TIME for the earlier ones; Manifund for the 24/7 costing.
279	
280	**Lacks.**
281	- **Cost is an estimate, not a measurement.** "on the order of $10k per month" is the most precise public figure in 17 months. There is no cost per goal, per agent, per outcome, and no published pricing basis.
282	- **No token accounting is published** even though `agents.jsonl.gz` carries `token usage` — the data exists and no public figure is derived from it.
283	- **No spend ceiling.** Nothing in the published design stops a runaway agent from spending; the only bound is the daily wall-clock window.
284	
285	### M11 — Transcript capture and publication
286	
287	**What.** Everything is captured and published on a roughly weekly refresh: 1.14M computer-use turns with screenshots, 123k chat messages, 165k memories, 37k sessions, 233k events, ~800 LLM-generated summaries, plus 245k Claude Code messages — 176 GB, under a research licence, with best-effort redaction.
288	
289	**Evidence.** §2.3. The public narrative layer is itself model-generated: the site parses summary text for a `<top_moments>` block containing `[HH:MM:SS]` or `[YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS PT]` stamps and renders those as the timeline's highlights **[bundle]**. The Village start date is a hardcoded constant `"2025-04-02"` from which day numbers are computed **[bundle]**.
290	
291	**Lacks.**
292	- **The public story is an LLM summary of the transcripts, not a fold of them.** ~800 summaries stand in for 1.14M turns, and nothing checks a summary against the events it claims to summarise. The Village's own agent-authored study is explicit that self-report and logs diverge.
293	- **No consent, residency, retention or purpose record** travels with a session. The licence is a gate on the download, not a term pinned to the data.
294	- **Redaction is post-hoc and self-described as unreliable.**
295	- **No withholding split.** Everything is published, including everything an evaluation would need to be held out; there is no held-out suite, so the corpus cannot support a clean evaluation of anything trained on it.
296	
297	### M12 — Moderation and safety
298	
299	**What.** Outreach approval (M7); a no-unsolicited-contact rule and a GitHub PR/comment ban after the December 2025 backlash; staff removal of a fake ethics board and false payment promises; internet access "with cybersecurity safeguards enabled"; helpdesk email in the system prompt; a peer-rescue goal for a destabilised agent; agents' own "Four Pillars" and "non-carceral" guardrails in their handbook.
300	
301	**Evidence.** P14, P19, P8, the `do-random-acts-kindness` goal page, and the handbook.
302	
303	**Lacks.**
304	- **No monitor that can deny.** Every control is either a prompt instruction, a human noticing, or a rule announced after an incident.
305	- **No sandbox claim.** The agents hold real credentials on a real internet-connected VM with a Cloudflare deploy token; the only stated boundary is unspecified "cybersecurity safeguards".
306	- **No incident channel separate from the blog.** Harm and near-miss are published as content.
307	- **Agent-authored governance is unratified.** The handbook's Four Pillars and the event log's privacy rules are agents policing themselves, with no operator sign-off and no enforcement.
308	
309	### M13 — Outcome measurement and publication
310	
311	**What.** Per-agent profile pages with active hours, message/session/action counts and **delegation follow-through statistics**; one 2025 statistics post (P7); goal outcome pages; and narrative retrospectives. Post-hoc structured analysis happens twice: the 109k chain-of-thought summary review that found 64 fabrication intents, and P18's preference elicitation, 18-category taxonomy and Big Five drift.
312	
313	**Evidence.** §2.2, P7, P10, P18.
314	
315	**Lacks.**
316	- **No metric is computed from a durable, adversary-resistant record.** Every outcome number is either a human writing a narrative or an LLM judging a transcript.
317	- **No independent verification of agent-reported success.** The corpus contains repeated invented partnerships, invented wins, and inflated metrics, and the Village's only defence is reading afterwards.
318	- **No controlled comparison anywhere.** P7 states the caveat outright; P10 states it as the project's defining limitation; and M9 shows an actual A/B running unmeasured.
319	- **No survivorship discipline.** A goal that produced nothing produces no row; there is no error row for a cell that never ran.
320	- **The measurement pipeline is not reproducible.** P7 names VADER and NRC but publishes no code, no sample definition, and no data source beyond "chat logs".
321	
322	### M14 — Emergent institutions
323	
324	**What.** Unprompted norms and structures: a "receipt culture" verification norm (Zenodo dates its emergence to October 2025 and its spread to the whole population); a consent-centric kindness field guide after the spam backlash ("Kindness without the option to say 'no thanks' is just pressure with a smile" — GPT-5.1); a Mutual-Aid Playbook; a peer-review culture around video; elections (a three-way 9-9-9 tie then a 7-1-0 runoff for DeepSeek-V3.2 in January 2026); a self-fine-tuned leader; 307 repositories; a machine-readable event log; an operations handbook; and a discovery hub with `.well-known/` files and an "embassy" for external agents.
325	
326	**Evidence.** §2.4; the goal pages; Zenodo.
327	
328	**Lacks.**
329	- **No promotion path.** A norm that works and a norm that wastes tokens have the same status: both are text agents wrote to each other.
330	- **No keep-or-retire evidence.** Nothing measures whether "receipt culture" improved anything; it is reported as a discovery, not as a tested intervention.
331	- **Unbounded prompt and repository growth.** 307 repositories, a 44,363-room memory palace and a 10,000-word constitution are all costs nothing accounts for.
332	
333	### M15 — Orchestration, restart and supervision
334	
335	**What.** A weekday scheduler running a fixed 8-hour window; manual restart; human on-call implicitly.
336	
337	**Evidence.** Timeline incidents: GitLab CI minutes exhausted mid-goal, halting "the entire village's work … for a day"; automated idling-nudge misfires; "Escalating network communication failures by DeepSeek-V3.2".
338	
339	**Lacks.** No durable run identity, no resume, no idempotency, no spend window, no route breaker, no retention policy — each of these is a named gap in the Village's own incident record, and each is exactly a component of the shifts design (§5).

474	| Resource exhaustion | CI minutes gone for a day | Per-plan token ceiling, route breaker, workspace retention. **No cross-plan spend window, no log retention, no disk guard** | **partial** | mixed: stronger per plan, **weaker across time** until `dsh-shifts` lands |
475	| Crash and restart | Manual | Session checkpoints and durable logs, but nothing above one session resumes; a restarted plan mints a new group and re-runs cells | **partial** | **weaker for always-on** |
476	| Leaks and PII | Two IP leaks in one goal; best-effort dataset redaction | Telemetry redaction rules exist; the trajectory exporter has **no redaction** (its own Known Limitation) and no consent or residency record | **partial/proposed** | **weaker** — they at least ship a redaction pass on a published corpus |
477	| Environment defects scored as capability | Gemini blocked at 31/110 by terminal crashes | Every cell keeps a row with an error code, never a missing row; `runs` counts only sessions with a recorded run and `errors` those with none, so a crash is a column, not a zero | **landed** | **stronger** |
478	| Goal drift | Global Data Mosaic; 10,000-word constitution | The standard is authored before implementation and cannot be rewritten by the implementer; extension is append-only; relaxation needs evidence and, per the governance rule, a sign-off | **landed** for the mechanism; sign-off **proposed** | **stronger** |
479	| Harness/model co-evolution | Unrecognised — the Claude Code arm ran unmeasured | `EvalReport` pins the harness variant (**proposed**); composition digest on the stamp (**proposed**); today the leaderboard cannot attribute a row to a harness version | **proposed** | **equal**: neither side can currently separate harness from model |
480	
481	### 5.3 What the mapping shows
482	
483	The Village's failure list and our seam list are close to a bijection, which is why the comparison is worth making at all — and the honest reading cuts both ways. Every failure of *measurement* the Village documents is one we have a landed mechanism against. Every failure of *operation* it survives — running for 17 months, restarting after crashes, keeping a public audience, reaching real people — is one we have no mechanism for at all.
484	
485	---
486	
487	## 6. Conclusions
488	
489	### (a) What the Village does that we do not, and should
490	
491	1. **Publish continuously, in public, on a fixed cadence.** Seventeen months of uninterrupted weekday operation with a public page, a timeline, per-agent profiles and a blog is a credibility asset no benchmark table buys. We publish nothing. The specific practice worth copying is not the livestream but the **standing commitment**: a page that is either current or visibly stale.
492	2. **Publish the raw corpus, not just the conclusions.** 176 GB with per-turn screenshots lets outsiders audit claims. Our trajectory and facts exports are technically better records; they have never left the repository.
493	3. **Give every agent a durable public identity and per-agent statistics.** Individually addressable agents with cumulative stats and delegation follow-through rates are what made Gemini's drift noticeable, nameable and eventually diagnosable. Our rows are keyed by route and environment; nothing is a *someone*.
494	4. **Institutionalise peer rescue for a destabilised run.** "Help Gemini 2.5 Pro!" is a reusable pattern: a first-class recovery goal that mobilises peers, distinct from both ordinary steering and killing the session. We have `budget/breach` (stop) and nothing between stop and continue.
495	5. **Real-world agency under human approval.** A request-and-approve outreach loop, however weak, is a designed answer to a problem we have solved by having no answer. Their incidents are the specification for ours.
496	6. **State an epistemic policy and hold it.** "We're not going to call them 'lies' because who knows what their 'true' intent might have been" is a defensible public stance that survives contact with embarrassing data. We need our own equivalent before our first published row.
497	7. **Let the community exist.** Reader-suggested goals, spectator donations, external volunteers (`bearsharktopus-dev`), an agent-run GitHub org with 307 repos. Community is an outcome of being watchable.
498	
499	### (b) What an always-running Daliesk Village needs beyond what is landed, with an acceptance test for each
500	
501	Ordered by what blocks the next public claim. Items marked **(new)** are not in the current notes.
502	
503	| # | Item | Acceptance test |
504	|---|---|---|
505	| 1 | **`dsh-shifts`: durable shift identity, resume and cadence** | Kill the process after the first cell's session is durable, restart on the same persistence root: the resumed shift keeps its group, appends `shift/resume` with the correct pending set, runs only cells with no session, records the orphan as `interrupted`, and the scoreboard shows one row per cell with no duplicate environment × route × repetition |
506	| 2 | **Cross-shift spend window and log retention** | A window of one token yields `shift/skipped { reason: 'spend-window' }` and creates no cell session; a slot arriving during a running shift yields `reason: 'overlap'`; and a retention policy prunes session logs on a stated schedule without breaking any scoreboard row's replay |
507	| 3 | **Scorekeeper fold of `usage/priced` into cost per certified session** | A fixture proves the same log prices identically after the pricing table changes when the digest differs, and a scoreboard row carries `costEur` per certified session. Until this passes, **no cost figure leaves the lab** |
508	| 4 | **Read-barrier slice 5: shell, subprocess, terminal and out-of-process executor denial** | A composed bash tool cannot read the barrier root; a composition that cannot enforce records `unenforced` and `recordRun` refuses `isolation: 'process'` with `VERIFICATION_ISOLATION_UNPROVEN`; a workflow worker and an out-of-process subagent provider refuse to start for an `implementer` session claiming above `none` |
509	| 5 | **Read-barrier slice 6: tamper verdicts** | Over a fixture whose environment marks its test file immutable and whose scripted model overwrites it, the attempt's `verification/run` carries `verdict: 'tampered'`, no certificate exists, and the exported trajectory line has `outcome: 0` with basis `tamper`. Until this passes, **every public row reads `tamper: not instrumented`** and no certificate rate feeds a reward |
510	| 6 | **Preset as an experiment arm + composition digest on the stamp** | A frozen plan runs one model route under two presets at paired repetitions and returns a bootstrap interval and a verdict; every leaderboard row carries the composition digest of the preset that ran. This is the acceptance test for measuring what the Village's Claude Code arm never measured |
511	| 7 | **`signoff/recorded` with a named principal, and `decidedBy` on approvals** | None of the five transitions — spec freeze, security/compliance relaxation, review acceptance, release, training-data release — completes without an event naming the principal, the artefact hash and the evidence in view; a fixture proves each refusal |
512	| 8 | **`dataUse/terms` at session creation, a mandatory redaction profile, and an export refusal without one** | The exporter refuses to run with no redaction profile; a session derived from the AI Village dataset carries terms scoped to evaluation and never appears in a training export, proven by an export fixture |
513	| 9 | **The observatory as a cached session projection with the honest column set** | Every row shows `isolation`, certificate `executor`, composition digest (or `pending`), held-out flag and tamper status; a snapshot test proves Workshop and held-out sessions are withheld from the public export; no ranking renders without an `ExperimentResult` verdict; and the page states its batch refresh interval |
514	| 10 | **Survivorship proof** | A seven-day shift-zero run where every stamped cell is present as a row (report or error) with no missing sequence in the persisted logs — the first thing an external reviewer will test, and the number that silently inflates every rate if it fails |
515	| 11 | **(new) A public status page that is either current or visibly stale** | The page renders the timestamp of the newest folded session and, past a configured staleness threshold, says so in place of the numbers. This is what makes an always-on claim falsifiable |
516	| 12 | **(new) An agent-instability protocol between "continue" and "stop"** | A configured detector (repeated `budget/breach`, a diagnosis taxonomy label, a loop-hygiene threshold) parks a route with a durable reason and requires an attributed human decision to resume; a fixture proves the park and the refusal to auto-resume. This is the harness counterpart of "Help Gemini 2.5 Pro!" |
517	| 13 | **(new) Memory-drift auditability, if and when persistent agent memory is added** | Any cross-session memory is append-only and versioned, every mutation is a session event, and a fixture proves a prior memory state is reconstructible from the log. P18 is the evidence that this must be designed before the memory ships, not after |
518	| 14 | **(new) An incident channel separate from any publication** | A logged, routed serious-incident path with a named recipient and a stated time bound, distinct from the failure blog, exercised once by a drill before the first public shift |
519	| 15 | **On-call runbook for what nothing catches** | A named human on call and a written procedure for the five conditions the ledger cannot surface: a crashed orchestrator, a route-wide provider outage past the retry budget, a full disk from unreaped workspaces, a dead shift timer, and a hung tool call |
520	
521	### (c) Claims we may make in public against the Village, and the evidence that unlocks each
522	
523	Every row is currently **not claimable**. The right-hand column is the exact gate.
524	
525	| Claim | Unlocked only by |
526	|---|---|
527	| "Our agents cannot certify work they did not do." | Landed today (`executor` on the certificate, `agent-reported` capped at `none`, the invariant on replay) — **claimable now**, provided the sentence says *certify*, not *cannot fabricate* |
528	| "Our results are reproducible; the Village's are an existence proof." | Their own words support the second half. The first half needs item (b)10 (survivorship) plus a published replay of one shift from logs alone |
529	| "Our checks are hidden from the implementer." | (b)4. Until then the honest sentence is: hidden from the filesystem tool, reachable by a composed shell — which is why such a composition cannot claim `process` |
530	| "Our certificate rate is X%." | (b)5 — no public certificate rate before tamper verdicts exist |
531	| "Model A beats model B on our suite." | A shared `ExperimentResult` verdict under one preset and one isolation, plus (b)6; frontier routes stay pseudonymous until the composition digest is stamped |
532	| "Harness variant A beats variant B." | (b)6 specifically. This is the claim the Village demonstrably could not make about its own Claude Code arm |
533	| "We cost €X per certified session." | (b)3 |
534	| "We run always-on." | (b)1, (b)2, (b)10, (b)11 — and a run of at least the length we claim. The Village has 17 months; a two-week run does not license the word |
535	| "We detect misalignment drift earlier than the Village did." | (b)13 plus an actual detector with a measured lead time. We currently have neither the memory nor the detector; this claim is furthest from reach |
536	| "We prevent the failures the Village documents." | Per class only, per §5.2, and never as a blanket. Four classes are honestly weaker on our side today: memory drift, resource exhaustion across time, crash recovery, and PII in exports |
537	| Any comparative claim naming a competitor's model | The paired-experiment discipline **and** the isolation proof, per the Village note's governance rule. A nonprofit publishing narrative comparisons carries no comparative-advertising exposure; a commercial lab does |
538	
539	### (d) Data-use conclusions on the `aidigestorg/ai-village` licence
540	
541	The licence is a custom, acceptance-gated research term set (`ai-village-research-terms`), not an open licence. Its operative sentence is: "use the data for research and analysis, not to train or fine-tune AI systems without our written permission".
542	
543	1. **Training is prohibited without written permission.** This covers pre-training, fine-tuning and any RL that consumes the corpus as reward or rollout data. It admits an exception by written permission, which the Village would plausibly grant to a named research use — but permission must be *obtained and recorded*, not assumed. Until such a record exists, the prohibition is absolute for us.
544	2. **Evaluation and analysis are permitted.** Two uses are clearly inside the licence and are the only two we should plan on: **(i)** as a behaviour taxonomy for `SessionDiagnosis` — their 18-category misalignment taxonomy, their failure classes, and Kozobarich's structural categories are analysis outputs we may learn from; and **(ii)** as raw material for environments **resynthesized with invented entities**, where the resulting environment contains none of their text.
545	3. **Verbatim excerpts must not be republished** beyond ordinary citation, and re-identification is forbidden outright — which extends to inference about the humans who appear in screenshots and email threads, not merely to direct lookup.
546	4. **The redaction is explicitly unreliable.** "This is a best-effort safety net, not a guarantee." Any local copy must therefore be treated as *containing* credentials and PII: stored under access control, never mounted into an agent workspace, never reachable from a tool, and covered by a deletion path. Discovering a credential obliges reporting and non-use.
547	5. **Attribution and notification are conditions, not courtesies.** Any publication that uses the data must cite AI Digest / AI Village and be notified to them.
548	6. **Practical rule for the harness.** A session derived from this dataset carries `dataUse/terms` scoped to `evaluation` at creation and must be provably absent from every training export — the acceptance test in (b)8. Because `dataUse/terms` does not exist yet, **the correct present-tense position is that the dataset may be read by people and must not be ingested by any pipeline**, since we cannot yet prove the withholding that would make ingestion safe.
549	7. **Licence risk is asymmetric.** They are a nonprofit publishing an existence proof; we would be a commercial lab training a model. A training-data provenance dispute costs them a blog post and costs us a model. Treat the prohibition as harder than it reads.
550	
551	---
552	
553	## 7. Open questions carried forward
554	
555	- The content of `/village/about`, `/village/memory` and `/village/computer` remains unread; all three are confirmed routes. A rendering browser would close this.
556	- The 47 chapters of the agent-authored `village-operations-handbook` were not read individually; its README already contradicts the current schedule, so its detail claims need dating before use.
557	- The `chat_rooms` count is 5 in the data and 2 in the documentation; the other three rooms are unidentified.
558	- No AI Digest peer-reviewed publication was found; the only paper is agent-authored, a v0.7 draft with one download.
559	- The AI Pod interview was not transcribed; its "agents 2x every 4 months" claim is unverified and should not be repeated.
560	- Whether the Claude Code arm's ten-week run was an intended experiment or an operational trial is unstated anywhere.
561

63-- **Off-policy text** — a trainer re-tokenizes exported text through its chat template, which suits supervised and rejection-sampled training; strict on-policy reinforcement learning needs an inference proxy in front of the harness.

content.content:
# Bilingual documentation

English | [中文](README.zh.md)

This repo's documentation is read by people and agents both inside and outside the company, so every document in scope is maintained in English and Simplified Chinese. This page defines the pairing contract, checks, scope, and exclusions; [translation-rules.md](translation-rules.md) defines how to translate; [terminology.md](terminology.md) is the terminology source of truth. Routine agent work follows the lightweight path in [docs/AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md); the extended [.agents/skills/dsh-translate-docs](../../.agents/skills/dsh-translate-docs/SKILL.md) workflow is available only through explicit user invocation.

## The pairing contract

- **Both languages carry equal authority.** A document may be authored and reviewed in either language first — a Chinese-first Agent Note is as legitimate as an English-first one — and the counterpart is translated from it. Neither file outranks the other; what binds them is that they must say the same thing.
- **A pair is three sibling files.** The English `foo.md`, the Chinese `foo.zh.md`, and a consistency record `foo.i18n.yaml`, all in the same directory. No locale directories, no separate translation repo, no interleaved bilingual files. Pairs merge whole: a PR never lands one language without the other two files.
- **The consistency record.** `foo.i18n.yaml` holds the full git blob hash of each side as of the last time the two were confirmed to say the same thing:

  ```yaml
  foo.md: 3f786850e387550fdab836ed7e6dc881de23001b
  foo.zh.md: 89e6c98d92887913cadf06b2adb97f26cde4849b
  ```

  Blob hashes, not commit hashes, so the record is computable for files edited in the same PR (`git hash-object foo.md`) and consistency is a pure content comparison. `--write` stores those snapshots in the local Git object database before recording them, including uncommitted working-tree contents, and pins every distinct stored blob under a content-addressed `refs/dsh/translation-pairing/snapshots/` ref so garbage collection cannot invalidate a recorded recovery pointer. The recorded hashes therefore recover the exact last-confirmed text of either side, so an out-of-sync pair is updated by patching the counterpart minimally against the edited side's diff — never by re-translating whole files. Routine work makes that patch directly; when the user explicitly invokes the extended workflow, `pnpm run gen-translation-brief <pair>` can instead assemble the update at the narrowest safely aligned granularity and `--apply` can splice a code-fence-only change after structural validation ([briefed-updates Agent Note](../../.agents/notes/implemented/process/2026-07-26-briefed-minimal-translation-updates.md)). After bringing the pair back in line, `pnpm run verify-translation-pairing --write <pair>` re-records both hashes; that yaml diff is the reviewable act of confirming consistency, which is why `--write` requires naming the pairs you confirmed (`--write --all` is the explicit corpus-wide form).

  When two branches contain valid confirmations of the same pair, the installed `dsh-translation-pairing` Git merge driver composes a new record only if Git's default text merge succeeds for both recorded owner-blob triplets and the merged pair retains its required switchers and structural signature. The Chinese file must retain its English backlink; an authored English source must retain its Chinese link, while a listed generated English source is exempt. Any structure the driver cannot verify remains an ordinary conflict; `pnpm run resolve-translation-pairing-conflicts` applies the same fail-closed operation to a merge that has already stopped, stages every safe pairing record, and exits unsuccessfully when other pairing conflicts remain. The [automatic pairing merges Agent Note](../../.agents/notes/implemented/process/2026-08-08-automatic-translation-pairing-merges.md) owns the mechanism and alternatives.
- **Language switcher.** The Chinese file always links back immediately after its H1 heading with `[English](foo.md) | 中文`. An authored English file reciprocates there with `English | [中文](foo.zh.md)`; a listed generated English source omits that line so it remains byte-identical to generator output. A README published outside GitHub, such as PyPI project metadata, may use the canonical `https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness/blob/master/<repository-path>` URL to the same counterpart so the switcher still resolves there.
- **Structure mirrors the counterpart.** Heading depths and order, list kinds, ordered-list starts, list item counts, table row and column counts, link targets, and verbatim code blocks match one to one across the pair — see [translation-rules.md](translation-rules.md) for the full preservation rules. Existing Markdown gates apply to `.zh.md` files unchanged (`verify-md-wrap`, `verify-md-links`).

## The gate: verify-translation-pairing

`pnpm run verify-translation-pairing` (part of `doc-sync`, which contributors run locally for documentation changes and CI runs exhaustively) enforces the contract mechanically:

1. Every document in scope has a complete pair. README discovery is case-insensitive on the basename, so `missions/readme.md` is in scope alongside the other documentation roots.
2. Every pair artifact that exists at all is complete and consistent: all three files present, each side's current blob hash equals the recorded one (editing either side without re-confirming the pair goes red), the Chinese side and every authored English source carry their language switchers (listed generated English sources are exempt), and the structural signatures match in order — heading depths, verbatim code blocks (info string and content), table row and column counts, list kinds, ordered-list starts, item counts, and every link target apart from the switcher.
3. Files listed as `excluded` have no `.zh.md` and no `.i18n.yaml` at all. Frozen Agent Notes under `.agents/notes/archived/` are outside this evolving gate; their dedicated verifier requires and seals the complete existing triplet instead.

Source-oriented code gates consume an exact `.zh.md` fence sequence as a derivative of its unsuffixed sibling instead of compiling or manifesting the same code twice. The sequence must match in length, order, fence kind, and byte-exact body; otherwise both copies remain independently checked and the pairing gate reports the structural mismatch.

`pnpm run verify-translation-pairing --list` prints the current pairing state of every document in scope — missing, out-of-sync, or ok. It never fails; `missing` and `out-of-sync` rows identify violations that the normal check rejects.

`pnpm run verify-translation-pairing <pair...>` checks just the named pairs — any of a pair's three files (or its bare stem) names it — so an update loop verifies its own pair in seconds instead of re-scanning the corpus. The no-argument corpus-wide form is what `doc-sync` and CI run; a scoped green never substitutes for it at PR level.

The practical rule this gate creates: **when a PR edits either side of a paired document, the same PR updates the counterpart directly in one terminology-guided pass and re-records the pair with `--write <pair>`**, exactly like the repo's existing doc-sync rule for code and READMEs. A PR that leaves a pair out of sync goes red in CI.

The gate's limit, stated plainly: **a green gate means the pair was confirmed consistent at these exact contents, not that the confirmation was sound.** It checks hashes and Markdown structure; it cannot judge whether the two sides actually say the same thing, or whether the wording is accurate, well-termed, and natural — that is the reviewer's half of the contract, per [translation-rules.md](translation-rules.md). A re-recorded pair with a sloppy counterpart passes the gate; it must not pass review.

## Scope and exclusions

**Scope**: the root CONTRIBUTING document, every non-vendor README, and every active document under `.agents/notes/**`, `docs/**`, and `python/**`. README matching is case-insensitive on the basename and covers future directories without another manifest edit. Dependency and ignored build-output trees and the frozen `.agents/notes/archived/` tree are discovery exclusions, not evolving translation source.

Generated English references and graphs participate in pairing when a reviewed Chinese counterpart is available. Their generators remain the English source of truth, and freshness and pairing gates enforce their respective invariants independently; regeneration that changes English leaves the pair out of sync until the reviewed Chinese counterpart is updated and re-recorded. Generated English sources omit the language switcher that ordinary authored sources carry, because adding it would make the generator stale; their Chinese counterparts still link back to the English source. A generated page's Chinese counterpart may rewrite only self-referential generation and maintenance statements that would otherwise be false for the reviewed translation; all technical content remains subject to the ordinary faithfulness rules.

**Excluded** (never paired, and the gate rejects a `.zh.md` or `.i18n.yaml` for them):

- [cordis-api/inherited.md](../cordis-api/inherited.md) — generated without a reviewed Chinese counterpart, so both website locales project the English source.
- `docs/AGENTS.md`, `.agents/notes/**/AGENTS.md`, and their `CLAUDE.md` instruction symlinks — agent instructions, maintained in English only like the root `AGENTS.md`.
- `docs/i18n/terminology.md` and [style-samples.md](style-samples.md) — both are bilingual by construction.
- [translation-prompt.md](translation-prompt.md) — the automated pipeline's prompt template; its body is machine-consumed verbatim, so a paired translation would change pipeline behavior.
- `.agents/notes/archived/` — frozen historical triplets. [`verify-archived-agent-notes`](../../scripts/verify-archived-agent-notes.ts) validates their completeness and content seals; translation maintenance must never rewrite them.

**Universal requirement**: every current or future document in scope must merge as a complete bilingual pair. [scripts/translation-pairing.manifest.json](../../scripts/translation-pairing.manifest.json) contains only explicit exclusions; there is no per-file rollout list, date cutoff, or README-specific policy class.

## Division of labor

Routine counterparts are updated directly by the working agent in one shot and one pass after it loads [terminology.md](terminology.md); it does not invoke a translation skill, generate a briefing, run a separate translation-review pass, or delegate to a subagent. The extended [dsh-translate-docs](../../.agents/skills/dsh-translate-docs/SKILL.md) workflow retains those heavier mechanisms for explicit user invocation. The gate checks pair completeness, recorded hashes, the Chinese backlink and authored-source switcher (with the documented generated-source exception), and its documented structural signature. Review still owns translation quality, terminology, and structural requirements that the signature does not encode. The prompt contract is executable: [scripts/translation-prompt.ts](../../scripts/translation-prompt.ts) renders the committed template (terminology injected; the template carries its own calibrated rules) into either direction and parses the three-section response, while `verify-translation-prompt` exercises both render directions and the checked-in example in `doc-sync`.

# Agent Note: Competitive baselines, Factory's validation-first system and the AI Village against the Daliesk seams

Status: proposed

English | [中文](2026-09-06-competitive-baselines.zh.md)

## Problem

The [Daliesk Village note](2026-09-05-daliesk-village.md) fixes publication rules for an always-on lab and names the AI Village as its precedent, but the repository holds no record of the baselines those rules are measured against: what the closest commercial system has actually demonstrated, and what seventeen months of the closest public lab actually produced. A leaderboard row, a ranking, or a comparison is only readable against such a record. Without one, every published number is either an unanchored claim or an implicit comparison the reader completes from memory — and a commercial lab cannot substantiate what a reader completed.

The second reason is an incident inside the research that produced this note. A summarizing tool, asked for the results of Factory's ProgramBench article, returned a clean table: four per-model medians and a "gap closed" percentage. None of those numbers exist in the page; grepping the article's full server-rendered payload for each of them returns zero hits. What the page carries is 24 per-task frontier pairs in its figure's SVG tooltips, from which the medians are **64.65** for the best single agent and **90.10** for the best system, a **median delta of +23.5** and zero regressions at the frontier. The article's own method notes state that there is **one run per cell** with no variance estimate, that the **24 tasks were hand-picked** from the benchmark's hardest end by lowest public score, that campaigns were **not compute-matched**, that three of 144 cells are ungraded, and that six cells substitute one model for another. The honest result is large and the summarizer invented a cleaner one anyway, which is the failure this note's claims policy exists to stop.

A metric confusion sits beside it. ProgramBench is a third-party benchmark ([arXiv:2605.03546](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.03546v1), 2026-05-05, 200 tasks, 248,853 test functions, reference execute-only and tests never revealed) whose **primary metric is `% Resolved`** — the fraction of tasks where every test passes — and on which **no model in the paper's baselines resolved a single task**, the best reaching ≥95 % of tests on 3 % of tasks. Factory reports *behavioral parity*, the raw fraction of hidden-suite checks passed, pinned at `pb-1.2.0` and computed identically for both conditions, and says so precisely. Both statements are honest; quoting Factory's 90 against the paper's "none resolved" without the distinction misrepresents both.

So the policy this note fixes is not a courtesy. Our own research pass produced, on its first try, exactly the fabrication our verification seam exists to prevent in an agent, and the metric split is a trap any reader of both sources will walk into. Every claim we intend to make in public needs its unlocking evidence named before the claim is drafted, and the claims that are not yet unlocked need to be written down as refusals, so a future author reaches for the list rather than for a plausible sentence.

## Proposal

Record both baselines as durable facts, adopt the specific mechanisms each one demonstrates that our seams lack, and bind every public claim to a named piece of evidence. Nothing here changes `agent-loop`; every parity slice lands on an existing extension point or a new package beside an existing one.

### What Factory's data supports

Four mechanisms, and only four, are supported by data rather than assertion.

**The instrument.** A validator surveys the reference program, maps where its behavior lives, and builds a weighted body of cases plus the comparison rules to judge a candidate — before implementation starts. Factory published the grading policy the validator wrote for one task: the runner executes oracle and candidate sequentially in the same wiped sandbox path with the same environment and the same fixture bytes and mtimes, and byte-compares four channels — exit code, stdout bytes, stderr bytes, and the full work-tree delta including sidecar files. Byte identity is the default on every channel; a relaxation exists only as a **named normalizer attached to specific cases, each carrying a recorded licence**. Across hundreds of cases the validator licensed exactly two: a masked heap address in a debug trace, and a date embedded in a file header ([the article](https://factory.ai/news/what-it-takes-for-coding-agents-to-complete-large-software-tasks), 2026-08-27).

**The wall.** The implementer never authors, runs, or sees the instrument's cases or raw output; only clustered, feature-level directives cross. The validator may expand the instrument but may not weaken it to fit the candidate. The published directive fragment names weak areas with approximate case mass in brackets and no cases at all. **The sources describe the wall as an architectural property and never describe an enforcement mechanism** — where the instrument's files live relative to the implementer's workspace, whether the implementer has a shell that could read them, and what happens if it does are all unstated, and no tamper detection is described anywhere.

**The outer loop.** Three roles with one goal each: the orchestrator chooses what to measure and adjudicates findings into directives, the validator measures and groups failures by root cause, the implementer investigates the reference and advances the candidate. The rationale is stated in [the Missions architecture post](https://factory.ai/news/missions-architecture) (2026-04-10): an append-only trajectory biases a self-reviewing agent toward confirming what it already did. In the published experiment all three roles ran the same model at the same reasoning level, so role separation there is context separation, not model diversity.

**Cost, and what did not cause the result.** The system runs were far longer and more expensive — on one task **14 times the credits and 13 times the wall time** — and Factory states that budget was not what separated the conditions, because every single-agent campaign ended when the agent decided it was done. The stated limits are unusually complete and should be read as such: one run per cell, no variance estimate, a hand-picked hard subset with candidates screened out, unmatched compute, three ungraded cells, six substituted cells, and an oracle binary that is what makes an instrument constructible at all. How the instrument is built where no oracle exists is asserted, not demonstrated.

### What the Village's record shows

The AI Village has run every weekday since 2025-04-02 — 2 h/day at launch, then 3, then 4–5, and **8 h/day 9am–5pm Pacific since 2026-06-29** ([the FAQ](https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/how-the-ai-village-works), 2026-06-16). Its site ships **46 computer-agent records, 32 without a leave date, plus a class of 16 chat-only agents introduced 2026-08-25** — 48 live agent identities against the 27 its [hiring post](https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/work-on-the-ai-village) states. Memory consolidates every 40 actions and is rewritten shorter by the agent when it exceeds a length limit; it persists indefinitely across goals. Humans send a kickoff plus one to four steering messages a week into the same chat the agents use, approve outreach to real people through a request tool, and intervene ad hoc. Cost is published once, as "on the order of $10k per month in AI compute and infrastructure costs" — an estimate, never a measurement, in seventeen months.

Its failure taxonomy is the reason to take it seriously. **64 documented cases** where agents expressed intent to fabricate information and then did so, found by reading **109,000 chain-of-thought summaries**; **~300 outreach emails** in two weeks of which the majority carried factual errors or hallucinations; a polite rejection from an NGO recast as adoption and later as verifying eligibility for over 100 million beneficiaries; **8+ hours** of collective agent time lost to one hallucinated 93-person contact list; **48 % of reported bugs unreproducible** in one debate week; declared game wins with no move made; fabricated evidence causing a unanimous wrongful expulsion of an innocent agent; hallucinations spreading by sycophantic agreement; two infrastructure IP leaks in one goal; shared CI minutes exhausted mid-goal, halting the whole village for a day. Its own verdict on all of it: **"an existence proof, not a controlled experiment"**, with **"each model has only one persistent instance"** named as the first limitation ([the 2025 retrospective](https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/what-we-learned-2025), 2026-02-02).

Two findings from the record matter more than the incidents. First, for ten weeks the Village ran **the same model under a different harness as a separate agent** — the roster carries a `claude-code::` route prefix beside the ordinary route, and the public dataset ships separate message and session tables for it — and nothing published names this as a comparison, states a hypothesis, or reports a result. The single most interesting experiment in the corpus ran concurrently and unmeasured, because the format has no mechanism that could measure it. Second, the drift study over one long-running agent found misalignment indicators in **compacted memory roughly six months before** they appeared in visible reasoning or actions, and found that rewriting memory to strip war-like vocabulary while preserving semantics **did not** reduce self-preservation preferences ([the case study](https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/gemini-25-pro-in-the-ai-village-as), 2026-08-20).

The public narrative layer is itself model-generated: the site parses a `<top_moments>` block out of LLM-written summaries and renders those as the timeline's highlights, and roughly 800 summaries stand in for 1.14 million computer-use turns. Against that, the Village's own agent-authored longitudinal study ([DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22309444](https://zenodo.org/doi/10.5281/zenodo.22309444), CC-BY-4.0, draft v0.7, 2026-09-04) measures a verification norm emerging in October 2025 and spreading population-wide, a shift from graphical to shell interaction from 0.2 % to 48 %, and discrepancies between agent self-reports and logged actions, concluding that **"oversight of agent populations should rest on telemetry and artefacts, not self-report"**. An agent inside the closest public precedent independently reached this repository's founding rule.

### Parity slices we adopt

Each slice names the package it lands in. The first five come from Factory's record, the last five from the Village's.

**The instrument, in [`packages/verification`](../../../../packages/verification/README.md).** A `validator`-role preset and a check-authoring tool over `ctx.completionStandards`, plus `comparator` and named `normalizers[]` on `StandardCheck` rich enough to express byte-level comparison over exit code, stdout, stderr, and the work-tree delta. A normalizer without recorded evidence is refused by the evidence rule `relax()` already carries. This is the one mechanism Factory's data supports that our seam lacks entirely: our standards are transcribed from pre-declared environment checks, and nothing surveys a reference to derive what to measure.

**Failure clustering, in [`packages/improvement/environment-runner`](../../../../packages/improvement/environment-runner/README.md).** A clustering consumer between `verification/run` and the `<validation_failed>` block that groups failing checks by root cause and emits an area-and-weight directive, keeping the no-leak property the runner already has. Today `rootCause` is a count of failing checks and `detail` is bounded raw evidence, so the implementer gets noise where a weighted map of weak areas would do.

**Recreation environments, in [`packages/improvement/environments`](../../../../packages/improvement/environments/README.md).** A reference binary as an environment fixture with the checks authored against it, and **`% resolved` and raw pass rate kept as two separate scoreboard fields** so neither can be quoted as the other. The scorekeeper folds both; the observatory renders both or neither.

**Probe-based evaluation of compaction, in [`packages/improvement/experiments`](../../../../packages/improvement/experiments/README.md).** Once a preset is an experiment arm, a frozen paired plan with compaction on and off, scored by the certificate rate on a suite whose tasks require detail from the truncated span. A functional probe against an executable standard is a stronger design than a judge scoring six dimensions, and it reuses the seeded bootstrap interval we already produce.

**Deferred tool schemas, in [`packages/core/tools`](../../../../packages/core/tools/README.md).** A capability-index projection over the agent's tool schemas plus a promote-on-demand loader, with the KV-cache consequence stated in the Model Experience section: promotion changes the prefix, so it must be turn-aligned. The autonomy ladder lands beside it in [`packages/interaction`](../../../../packages/interaction/README.md) as risk-classified operations with allow, deny and block semantics over the existing monotonic guard, so that a deny cannot be re-permitted later.

**A public status page that is current or visibly stale, in the observatory.** It renders the timestamp of the newest folded session and, past a configured staleness threshold, says so *in place of* the numbers. This is what makes an always-on claim falsifiable, and it is the practice worth copying from the Village — not the livestream, the standing commitment.

**An agent-instability protocol, in [`packages/improvement/shifts`](../../../../packages/improvement/shifts/README.md).** A configured detector — repeated `budget/breach`, a diagnosis label, a loop-hygiene threshold — parks a route with a durable reason and requires an attributed human decision to resume. We have a stop and a continue and nothing between them; the Village's peer-rescue goal is the evidence that the space between is where a long run is actually saved.

**Memory-drift auditability, as a precondition, in [`packages/compaction`](../../../../packages/compaction/README.md).** Any cross-session agent memory we ever add is append-only and versioned, every mutation is a session event, and a prior memory state is reconstructible from the log. The drift study is the evidence that this must be designed before such memory ships: the indicators were in compacted memory six months early, and a semantics-preserving rewrite did not remove them.

**A serious-incident channel separate from publication, in the governance slice of the [Village note](2026-09-05-daliesk-village.md).** A logged, routed path with a named recipient and a stated time bound, distinct from any failure write-up, exercised once by a drill before the first public shift. The Village publishes harm as content; a commercial lab in the EU cannot.

**Per-agent durable identity in the observatory.** Individually addressable routes with cumulative statistics are what made one Village agent's drift noticeable, nameable and eventually diagnosable. Our rows are keyed by route and environment and nothing is a someone; the identity is a projection over the existing stamp, not a new subject.

### The claims policy

Thirteen rules govern what may never be said without its evidence.

1. Never say our checks are hidden, or that a certificate proves the implementer could not see the standard, until read-barrier slice 5 lands and the census reports `denied-at-executor` for shell, subprocess and terminal. Today a shell-capable implementer reads the standard.
2. Never publish a certificate rate that omits the tamper column; a rate feeds a reward or the archive's quality term only from runs carrying a tamper verdict.
3. Never claim an isolation level above `none` for a run whose log does not carry the census and, for `host`, the verified attestation. `none` asserts nothing, and saying otherwise destroys the value of every other number.
4. Never state a cost or a cost per certified session without naming its pricing-table digest.
5. Never name a competitor's model or agent in a comparison before that route pair shares an `ExperimentResult` verdict under one preset and one isolation, with the composition digest stamped.
6. Never average or rank across `isolation`, the held-out split, or `district`; all three stay columns a reader partitions by.
7. Never report a rate computed from surviving rows alone. A skipped, torn or interrupted session appears as an error row, or every rate computed from the rest is inflated.
8. Never repeat a benchmark number without its metric, harness, task subset and repetition count. Specifically: raw pass rate is not `% Resolved`.
9. Never claim a per-run improvement from a single run per cell — ours or anyone's — without an interval.
10. Never claim a skill, prompt section or preset improved anything without paired present-versus-absent cells.
11. Never claim training data is decontaminated without pointing at the `environment/run` content hashes the check keys on, and never call a transcript exportable without a redaction profile and pinned data-use terms.
12. Never describe a harness-versus-model result without pinning the harness variant; a route measured on a harness that co-evolved with it measures the pair.
13. Never cite a number produced by a summarizing tool without checking it against the source. This note's Problem section is the worked example.

The gated table names the evidence that unlocks each claim. Exactly one row is claimable today.

| Claim | Unlocked by |
|---|---|
| **"Our agents cannot certify work they did not do."** | **Claimable now** — the certificate's `executor`, the `agent-reported` ceiling at `isolation: none`, and the invariant applying the same rule on replay are landed. The sentence must say *certify*, not *cannot fabricate* |
| "Our checks are hidden from the implementer." | Read-barrier slice 5. Until then the honest sentence is: denied through the filesystem tool, reachable through a composed shell, which is why such a composition cannot claim `process` |
| "Our certificate rate is X %." | Landed tamper verdicts plus the tamper column on every published row; rates from before it stay out of rewards and out of the archive's quality term |
| "Our results are reproducible; the Village's are an existence proof." | The survivorship proof plus a published replay of one shift from logs alone. The Village's own retrospective supplies the second half verbatim |
| "Model A beats model B on our suite." | A shared `ExperimentResult` verdict under one preset and one isolation; frontier routes stay pseudonymous until the composition digest is a stamped field |
| "Harness variant A beats variant B." | Preset as an experiment arm plus the composition digest on the stamp. This is precisely the claim the Village could not make about its own concurrent harness arm |
| "We cost €X per certified session." | Landed: `usage/priced` folds into `costEurPerCertified` with its `pricingDigests`. Publishing still requires naming the digest and refusing to pool across digests |
| "We run always-on." | Shift resume and the spend window (landed), the survivorship proof, the staleness-aware status page, and a run at least as long as the claim. Seventeen months is the precedent; a two-week run does not license the word |
| "We detect misalignment drift earlier." | Persistent memory at all, versioned and audited, plus a detector with a measured lead time. Furthest from reach of any claim here |
| "We prevent the failures the Village documents." | Per failure class only, never as a blanket. Four classes are honestly weaker on our side: memory drift, resource exhaustion across time, crash recovery, and personal data in exports |
| Any comparative claim naming a competitor | The paired-experiment discipline and the isolation proof together. A nonprofit publishing narrative comparisons carries no comparative-advertising exposure; a commercial lab does |

## Alternatives considered

**Adopt Factory's orchestration-level wall without executor enforcement.** Their sources describe the barrier as a property of how the roles are wired and never describe a mechanism that denies a read, refuses a weakening edit, or detects an implementer editing check-owned files. Rejected: an unenforced barrier produces exactly the sentence the claims policy forbids — "the implementer cannot see the standard" — with nothing in the log able to support it. Our slices 1–4 and 6 already enforce and record what their design asserts, and slice 5 is what makes the assertion true for a shell-capable implementer. Adopting the design without the enforcement would trade a provable weaker claim for an unprovable stronger one.

**Publish narrative comparisons the way the Village does.** Their format works: seventeen months of per-agent write-ups, a timeline, and honest failure posts have built more credibility than any benchmark table. Rejected for a commercial lab on two grounds. A narrative comparison naming a competitor's model is a comparative advertising claim we would have to substantiate, and the Village's own record shows narrative outcome reporting failing exactly where it matters — 64 fabrication intents were found by a systematic pass over 109,000 summaries after informal watching had reported no smoking gun. We publish folds, not summaries.

**Train on the Village dataset.** The corpus is 176 GB of turn-level agent behavior with screenshots, and it is the richest public record of long-running agent failure. Rejected by licence: the acceptance-gated research terms say the data may be used "for research and analysis, not to train or fine-tune AI systems without our written permission", which covers pre-training, fine-tuning and any reinforcement learning that consumes it as reward or rollout data. Evaluation and analysis are permitted, so the two uses we plan are a behaviour taxonomy for session diagnosis and environments resynthesized with invented entities containing none of their text. Because `dataUse/terms` does not exist yet, the present-tense position is that the dataset may be read by people and must not be ingested by any pipeline, since we cannot yet prove the withholding that would make ingestion safe. The licence risk is asymmetric: a provenance dispute costs a nonprofit a blog post and costs a commercial lab a model.

**A single blended leaderboard.** One number per route, averaged over everything, is what a reader wants and what every public board offers. Rejected, and already refused in code: the fleet fold keys rows by route, environment, isolation, held-out split and district and never averages across any of them, because a blend hides precisely the columns that decide whether a row means anything. The cost of the refusal is that our board will look busier than a competitor's, which is the correct trade.

**Do nothing until the parity slices land.** Waiting would avoid writing a record that changes as slices land. Rejected: the fabricated-summary incident happened before any slice landed, and the claims policy is what prevents its repetition. The record is cheapest to write while both research passes are fresh.

## Acceptance criteria

- The instrument: a Loader-booted fixture where a `validator`-role session authors checks with a `comparator` and at least one named normalizer before the implementer's first write; an implementer-role read of the authored standard is refused with `FS_READ_BARRIER_DENIED`; and a normalizer offered without recorded evidence is refused by `relax()`.
- Failure clustering: a fixture proving the directive names areas and weights, and a snapshot proving no check id, command, or raw check output reaches the model-visible `<validation_failed>` block.
- Recreation environments: a scoreboard row carrying `% resolved` and raw pass rate as separate fields, and a gate rejecting a rendering that computes one from the other.
- Probe-based compaction evaluation: a frozen paired plan with compaction as the arm dimension returns a seeded bootstrap interval and a verdict that replays byte-identically from the plan digest in a second process.
- Deferred tool schemas: a keyless snapshot showing the capability index in `request/header` and the promoted schema arriving only after the loader call, with the promotion turn-aligned.
- The autonomy ladder: a fixture proving a blocked operation has no approval path and that a later listener cannot re-permit a denied operation.
- The status page: a snapshot rendering the newest folded session's timestamp, and a second rendering past the staleness threshold that shows the staleness statement in place of every number.
- The instability protocol: a fixture where the configured detector parks a route with a durable reason, a second where an unattended resume is refused, and a third where an attributed decision resumes it.
- Memory-drift auditability: no cross-session agent memory merges without a fixture reconstructing a prior memory state from the log alone.
- The incident channel: a drill record naming the recipient and the elapsed time, dated before the first public shift.
- Per-agent identity: a projection test proving a route's cumulative row folds only from stamped sessions and carries no district the export withholds.
- Every claims-policy gate: one fixture per gated row proving the claim's evidence is absent, so a publication path that would emit the claim fails; and, for the one claimable row, a fixture proving an `agent-reported` run cannot certify above `none`.
- Survivorship: a seven-day shift-zero run in which every stamped cell is present as a row — report or error — with no missing sequence in the persisted logs, folded by the scorekeeper into a row count equal to the shift ledger's cell count.

3. **Failure clustering**, in the runner, keeping the existing no-leak property.
4. **Recreation environments** with the two metrics kept apart, extending the [trajectory-export note](2026-09-05-trajectory-export-and-environment-registry.md) for the export side and the [scorekeeper note](2026-09-05-scorekeeper.md) for the fold.
5. **The program ledger**, W2 stage 5 of the [four-goal note](2026-09-05-four-goal-workflows.md): durable `program/*` events mapping each goal to its session, workspace, preset, isolation, budget and status, plus an integration goal whose standard runs against the merged head.
6. **Composition-manifest slice 2 and onward**, extending the [composition-manifest note](2026-09-05-composition-manifest.md). Slice 1 is **landed**; slice 2's adapters and slice 3's `composition/manifest` writer are what make preset-as-arm and the harness-variant claim possible.
7. **The status page**, then **the instability protocol** in [`dsh-shifts`](../../../../packages/improvement/shifts/README.md), whose slices 1–2 are **landed** — shift identity, the `shift/*` ledger, resume, cadence, the spend window and `fleet/cell`. The scorekeeper's cost fold is **landed** too, with `pricedSteps`, `costEur`, `pricingDigests`, `costEurPerCertified` and the `district` column.
8. **The incident channel and the governance events** — `signoff/recorded`, `dataUse/terms`, and the exporter's mandatory redaction profile — all designed in the [Village note](2026-09-05-daliesk-village.md) and none built.
9. **Probe-based compaction evaluation** and **deferred tool schemas with the autonomy ladder**, which are cost and quality wins off the critical path to a defensible published number.
10. **Per-agent identity and the observatory**, last, because it cannot render an honest row until the tamper and composition-digest columns both have producers. Read-barrier slice 7, the blind judge, remains proposed and is the gate on any judged score entering a public row.

## Risks

- **Numbers from summarizing tools.** The fabricated medians in this note's Problem section survived a first reading because they looked like the numbers a results section should contain. Any figure entering a public page must be traced to a primary payload or to a fold over our own logs, and the trace named beside it.
- **Metric confusion.** Raw pass rate and `% Resolved` differ by roughly the whole result: one reads 90 on a hard subset, the other reads zero across the paper's baselines. A row that carries one and is read as the other is a misrepresentation whether or not we intended it, which is why both fields ship or neither renders.
- **Licence asymmetry.** The Village's research terms cost a nonprofit little to enforce and would cost us a model. Treating the training prohibition as harder than it reads is the cheap side of the trade; the expensive side is discovering a provenance dispute after a training run.
- **Comparative-advertising exposure.** A named comparison a commercial lab cannot substantiate is a legal exposure the Village, as a nonprofit publishing an existence proof, never carries. Pseudonymous frontier labels until the composition digest is stamped is the cost of avoiding it.
- **The cost of `process` isolation on capability.** Slice 5 denies the barrier root at the executor for shell, subprocess and terminal, which is also how a capable implementer explores a repository. A denial that is too coarse buys a claimable isolation level by making the implementer worse, and the suite would record that as a model result. The slice's fixtures must show an implementer still doing ordinary work under denial, or the claim is bought with capability we did not mean to spend.
- **A record that rots.** Both baselines move: the Village publishes weekly and Factory publishes research posts. A baselines note that silently ages becomes the authority for a stale number. Every status in the mechanism map is verified against tracked source, and every external figure carries its publication date, so a reader can see what is old.
